entries.title: camt.029 Explained
entries.text: camt.029 Explained camt.029 Explained What it is The camt.029 is the Resolution of Investigation message. It is an ISO 20022 message that a bank sends to answer an investigation about a payment. The most common investigations it answers are cancellation requests, but it is also used to answer other payment investigations, such as a request to confirm whether a payment was received, or a request to correct payment details. The camt.029 is the second half of a conversation. The first half is the investigation request: a camt.056 FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request or a camt.055 Customer Payment Cancellation Request . The camt.029 is the reply. It tells the requesting bank what happened: whether the cancellation was accepted, whether it is still being processed, or whether it was rejected and why. entries.title: camt.056 Explained
entries.text: camt.056 Explained camt.056 Explained What it is The camt.056 is the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request. It is an ISO 20022 message that one financial institution sends to another to ask for a payment instruction to be cancelled. The bank that sent the payment uses it when it discovers, after sending the instruction, that the payment should not have been sent, or should not go ahead as instructed. The camt.056 is sent between banks, not by customers. A customer who wants to cancel a payment tells their own bank. The bank then decides whether a cancellation is possible and, if so, sends the camt.056 to the next bank in the chain. The customer never sees the camt.056 itself. A cancellation request is not the same as a return. A return, sent as a pacs.004, is used when the beneficiary bank cannot credit the payment and sends the money back on its own initiative. entries.title: camt Messages Explained
entries.text: camt Messages Explained camt Messages Explained What it is camt messages are the ISO 20022 messages for cash management . The name comes from Cash Management, and the messages cover account statements, notifications, investigations and cancellations. While pacs messages move payments and pain messages initiate them, camt messages tell banks what happened to the money. The five camt messages a payments professional must know are camt.052 , camt.053 , camt.054 , camt.056 and camt.029 . Each has a distinct job, and confusing them is a common source of errors. Why it matters camt messages matter because they are how a bank knows its own position. The statement tells the bank what was debited and credited. The notification tells it a payment has arrived. The cancellation request is how it asks for money back. The investigation response is how it resolves a query. Without camt messages, a bank would be blind to its own accounts. entries.title: ISO 20022 Explained: the Global Standard for Payment Messages
entries.text: ISO 20022 Explained: the Global Standard for Payment Messages ISO 20022 Explained: the Global Standard for Payment Messages ISO 20022 is the international standard for exchanging financial messages between banks. It defines the common language that payments, securities, trade, cards and foreign exchange messages are written in, and it is the standard every modern payment system now runs on, from SEPA and TARGET Services to CHAPS, Fedwire and SWIFT cross-border payments. What it is ISO 20022 is an international standard for exchanging financial messages between banks and other financial institutions. It defines a common language for payments, securities, trade, cards and foreign exchange. The messages are written in XML , a structured text format that machines can read and validate. entries.title: ISO 20022 Interview Questions
entries.text: ISO 20022 Interview Questions ISO 20022 Interview Questions Q1. Explain ISO 20022 to a non-technical stakeholder. Why did the industry move to it? ISO 20022 is a common language for financial messages. Before it, banks used MT messages, which are short text blocks with limited data. A beneficiary address was four lines of free text, and every bank read it differently. ISO 20022 replaces that with structured data: the address is broken into street, town, country and postcode, and the remittance information is structured so the beneficiary can reconcile automatically. The industry moved because regulators want better data for sanctions screening, corporates want automatic reconciliation, and banks want fewer errors. The move is not just a format change. It is a data quality change, and that is the point to make to a stakeholder. Q2. A pacs.008 payment is rejected with reason code AC01. What happened and what do you do? entries.title: MT to MX Field Mapping
entries.text: MT to MX Field Mapping MT to MX Field Mapping What it is MT to MX field mapping is the translation of each field in a SWIFT MT message into the equivalent element in an ISO 20022 MX message, and back again. MT messages are the older SWIFT format: fixed text blocks with numbered fields, such as field 59 for the beneficiary. MX messages are the newer ISO 20022 format: structured XML with named elements, such as the Cdtr block for the creditor. Mapping is the core work of the migration from MT to MX. A bank cannot send a pacs.008 until it knows how each MT103 field becomes a pacs.008 element. It cannot receive a pacs.008 until it knows how each element maps back to the fields its downstream systems expect. And during the coexistence period, it must translate in both directions, because some counterparties send MT and others send MX. entries.title: MT to MX Migration
entries.text: MT to MX Migration MT to MX Migration What it is MT to MX migration is the move from SWIFT MT messages to ISO 20022 MX messages for cross-border payments and reporting. MT messages are the older SWIFT format: fixed text blocks with numbered fields, such as field 59 for the beneficiary. MX messages are the newer ISO 20022 format: structured XML with named elements. The migration is driven by CBPR+ , the Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus programme, which is SWIFT's framework for moving the cross-border community to ISO 20022. The programme started in November 2022 with a coexistence period, during which banks could send either MT or MX messages. The coexistence period was extended, and the migration continues as banks complete their own cutovers. Why it matters The migration matters because MT messages cannot carry the data that modern payments need. MT fields are short, unstructured, and interpreted differently by different banks. entries.title: pacs.002 Explained
entries.text: pacs.002 Explained pacs.002 Explained What it is pacs.002 is the Payment Status Report message. It is the ISO 20022 message a bank sends to tell the previous bank what happened to a payment. The name comes from the ISO 20022 message set: pacs stands for Payments Clearing and Settlement, and 002 is the status report variant. Every pacs.008 or pacs.009 that a bank sends should receive a pacs.002 in reply. The pacs.002 carries a status code and, if the payment was rejected, a reason code that explains why. It is the single most important message for payment tracking, because it is how the sending bank knows whether the payment succeeded. Why it matters pacs.002 matters because a payment is not done when it is sent. It is done when the receiving bank confirms it. Without the pacs.002, the sending bank does not know whether the payment was accepted, is still being processed, was settled, or was rejected. entries.title: pacs.004 Explained
entries.text: pacs.004 Explained pacs.004 Explained What it is pacs.004 is the Payment Return message. It is the ISO 20022 message a bank sends to return funds that have already settled. The name comes from the ISO 20022 message set: pacs stands for Payments Clearing and Settlement, and 004 is the payment return variant. A return is different from a rejection. A rejection happens before settlement, when no money has moved. A return happens after settlement, when the money has already been credited and now needs to come back. The pacs.004 is a real payment in reverse: it moves funds from the beneficiary bank back to the sending bank. Why it matters pacs.004 matters because settled payments sometimes need to come back. The beneficiary account may be closed, the beneficiary may have returned the goods, the payment may have been sent in error, or a recall may have been accepted. In all these cases, the money cannot simply be cancelled. It has to travel back through the payment chain, and the pacs.004

entries.title: pacs.008 Explained: the ISO 20022 Customer Credit Transfer Message
entries.text: pacs.008 Explained: the ISO 20022 Customer Credit Transfer Message pacs.008 Explained: the ISO 20022 Customer Credit Transfer Message pacs.008 is the ISO 20022 message banks use to send a customer credit transfer to another bank. It is the message that carries a cross-border payment from one bank to the next, with the amount, the parties, the charges and the remittance detail, and it is the message every payments BA meets first when they work on cross-border payments, SEPA, or SWIFT gpi tracking. What it is pacs.008 is the Financial Institution to Financial Institution Customer Credit Transfer message. It is the ISO 20022 message a bank sends to another bank to move money on behalf of a customer. The name comes from the ISO 20022 message set: pacs stands for Payments Clearing and Settlement, and 008 is the customer credit transfer variant. When a customer instructs a cross-border payment, their bank builds a pacs.008 and sends it to the next bank in the chain, usually a correspondent

entries.title: pacs.009 Explained
entries.text: pacs.009 Explained pacs.009 Explained What it is pacs.009 is the Financial Institution to Financial Institution Credit Transfer message. It is the ISO 20022 message a bank sends to another bank to move its own money, or money on behalf of another bank, where there is no underlying customer payment. The name comes from the ISO 20022 message set: pacs stands for Payments Clearing and Settlement, and 009 is the bank to bank credit transfer variant. The key difference from pacs.008 is that pacs.009 has no customer behind it. It moves money between financial institutions. Typical uses are a bank funding its own account at another bank, a bank settling a position, a cover payment moving funds to support a customer payment, and a bank paying another bank for a service. Why it matters pacs.009 matters because banks move large amounts of their own money every day, and those movements need the same rigour as customer payments. entries.title: pain.001 Explained
entries.text: pain.001 Explained pain.001 Explained What it is pain.001 is the Customer Credit Transfer Initiation message. It is the message a customer uses to tell their bank to make a credit transfer. The name comes from the ISO 20022 message set: pain stands for Payment Initiation, and 001 is the credit transfer initiation variant. A corporate customer sends a pain.001 to its bank, usually as a file containing many payments, or as a single payment from an online banking or ERP system. A retail customer does not normally see pain.001, because their bank builds it internally from the online banking instruction. But the message is the same: it is the instruction that starts a credit transfer. Why it matters pain.001 matters because it is the first message in the payment chain. Everything downstream depends on it being correct. If the debtor account is wrong, the payment debits the wrong account. entries.title: Correspondent Banking Explained: How Banks Pay Each Other Across Borders
entries.text: Correspondent Banking Explained: How Banks Pay Each Other Across Borders Correspondent Banking Explained: How Banks Pay Each Other Across Borders What it is Correspondent banking is the system that lets banks move money across borders when they do not have a direct relationship with each other. A bank in one country holds an account with a bank in another country. That account is called a nostro account . The bank holding the account is the respondent bank. The bank that holds the account for them is the correspondent bank. When a customer of the respondent bank wants to pay someone in the correspondent bank's country, the respondent bank instructs the correspondent bank to make the payment from the nostro account. The correspondent bank debits the nostro account and pays the beneficiary. This is how most cross-border payments work. Correspondent banking is the backbone of international payments. Without it, a bank could only pay beneficiaries in countries where it has its own branch

entries.title: MT101 Explained: The Request for Transfer
entries.text: MT101 Explained: The Request for Transfer MT101 Explained: The Request for Transfer What it is The MT101 is the SWIFT message a customer or a bank sends to instruct another bank to debit an account and make one or more payments. It is a request for transfer . Unlike the MT103, which is a single payment instruction from one bank to another, the MT101 is an instruction from a customer to their bank, or from one bank to another bank, to execute payments on their behalf. The MT101 is most commonly used for bulk payments . A company that needs to pay hundreds of suppliers, or pay salaries to thousands of employees, sends a single MT101 containing many individual payment instructions. The bank reads the MT101, debits the company account, and executes each payment. The MT101 is also used by banks to instruct other banks to make payments from an account the instructing bank holds with them. It is a versatile message, but it is less common than the MT103 in everyday cross-border payments. Why

entries.title: MT103 Explained: The Single Customer Credit Transfer
entries.text: MT103 Explained: The Single Customer Credit Transfer MT103 Explained: The Single Customer Credit Transfer What it is The MT103 is the SWIFT message a bank sends to move money for a customer to another bank. It is a single customer credit transfer . When a person or a company asks their bank to pay someone in another country, the bank sends an MT103 to the next bank in the chain. The message carries the instruction to pay, the amount, the currency, who is sending, and who should receive the money. This guide explains the MT103 format field by field, with a worked MT103 example, the MT103 to pacs.008 mapping, and the common mistakes that send MT103 payments to repair. If you are searching for what an MT103 is, how to read one, or what fields 50a, 59a and 71A mean, this page answers all three. The MT103 is the workhorse of cross-border customer payments. entries.title: MT202 COV Explained: The Cover Payment with Full Transparency
entries.text: MT202 COV Explained: The Cover Payment with Full Transparency MT202 COV Explained: The Cover Payment with Full Transparency What it is The MT202 COV is the SWIFT message a bank sends to move funds as cover for a customer payment, with the full customer details included. COV stands for cover. The MT202 COV is a variant of the MT202. The difference is that the MT202 COV carries fields 50a ordering customer and 59a beneficiary customer , so every bank in the chain can see who is sending the money and who is receiving it. The MT202 COV exists because of a transparency problem. In the cover method, the customer payment instruction the MT103 goes directly to the beneficiary bank, while the funds travel separately through the correspondent chain. The intermediary banks moving the funds could not see the customer details. They were moving money blind. entries.title: MT202 Explained: The General Financial Institution Transfer
entries.text: MT202 Explained: The General Financial Institution Transfer MT202 Explained: The General Financial Institution Transfer What it is The MT202 is the SWIFT message a bank sends to move money to another bank for its own account. It is a general financial institution transfer . Unlike the MT103, which carries a customer payment, the MT202 moves funds between banks themselves. It is used for bank-to-bank transfers, funding a nostro account, settling a position, or paying another bank. The MT202 is also used as a cover payment . When a bank sends a customer payment by the cover method, it sends the MT103 directly to the beneficiary bank and sends an MT202 through the correspondent chain to move the funds. The standard MT202 used as cover does not carry customer details. The MT202 COV is the variant that does carry them, and it is the one banks must use for customer payment cover. Why it matters The MT202 is the message that actually moves money between banks in many cross-border payments.

entries.title: Nostro vs Vostro: The Same Account, Two Perspectives
entries.text: Nostro vs Vostro: The Same Account, Two Perspectives Nostro vs Vostro: The Same Account, Two Perspectives What it is Nostro and vostro are two names for the same bank account, seen from different sides. The words come from Latin. Nostro means "ours". Vostro means "yours". A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with a correspondent bank in another country. From the perspective of the bank that owns the account, it is "our account with you". A bank in India that holds a US dollar account with a bank in New York calls that account its nostro account. A vostro account is the same account, seen from the perspective of the bank that holds it for the other bank. From the perspective of the New York bank, the Indian bank's account is a vostro account, meaning "your account with us". It is the same account. The name changes depending on who is talking. Why it matters Nostro and vostro accounts are the foundation of correspondent banking and cross-border payments. Every time your bank

entries.title: OUR, SHA and BEN Explained
entries.text: OUR, SHA and BEN Explained OUR, SHA and BEN Explained What it is OUR, SHA, and BEN are the three charge options for a cross-border payment. They decide who pays the charges that the banks in the payment chain apply. The option is agreed between the sender and their bank before the payment is sent, and it is carried in the payment message so that every bank in the chain knows who should pay it. The three options work like this: - OUR means the sender pays all the charges. Every bank in the chain charges the sender, and the beneficiary receives the full amount. In the MT103, this is field 71A with the code OUR. In the pacs.008, it is the charge bearer code DEBT , which means the charges are borne by the debtor. - SHA means the charges are shared: the sender pays the sending bank charge, and the correspondent and beneficiary bank charges are deducted from the amount in transit, so the beneficiary receives less than the instructed amount. In the MT103, this is field 71A with the code SHA.

entries.title: Serial vs Cover Payments: Two Ways to Move Money Across Borders
entries.text: Serial vs Cover Payments: Two Ways to Move Money Across Borders Serial vs Cover Payments: Two Ways to Move Money Across Borders What it is When a bank sends a cross-border payment, the funds have to travel from the sender bank to the beneficiary bank. There are two ways to do this: the serial method and the cover method . The choice affects speed, cost, transparency, and risk. In the serial method , a single message travels from bank to bank along the chain. Each bank receives the payment instruction, deducts its charges if any, and forwards the remaining amount to the next bank. The instruction and the funds travel together, hop by hop, until they reach the beneficiary bank. In the cover method , two messages travel separately. The payment instruction the MT103 or pacs.008 goes directly from the sender bank to the beneficiary bank. The funds travel separately through the correspondent banking chain, carried by a cover message the MT202 COV or pacs.009 . The beneficiary bank receives

entries.title: SWIFT gpi Explained
entries.text: SWIFT gpi Explained SWIFT gpi Explained What it is SWIFT gpi Global Payments Innovation is a service that runs on top of the SWIFT network and gives banks and their customers end-to-end visibility of a cross-border payment. Before gpi, a cross-border payment disappeared into a chain of correspondent banks. The ordering bank could not see where the payment was, how long it would take, or what charges had been deducted. The customer asking "where is my payment" got no useful answer. gpi changed that by adding tracking, speed commitments, and fee transparency to the same SWIFT messages banks already used. gpi is not a new payment system and it is not a new message type. It is a set of rules and services that gpi member banks agree to follow. The core of it is the UETR , the Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference, a 36-character identifier that stays with a payment for its whole journey. Every bank in the chain includes the UETR in its status reports, so the payment can be followed from

entries.title: SWIFT Payments Explained
entries.text: SWIFT Payments Explained SWIFT Payments Explained What it is A SWIFT payment is a cross-border payment that travels over the SWIFT network. SWIFT is a member-owned cooperative that runs a secure messaging network for financial institutions. More than 11,000 institutions in over 200 countries use it. When a bank sends a payment to a bank in another country, it usually sends the instruction over SWIFT. Three facts about SWIFT surprise most newcomers. First, SWIFT is a messaging network, not a bank . It does not hold money, it does not settle payments, and it does not move funds. It carries instructions between banks. Second, SWIFT does not move the money behind the instruction. The funds move separately, through nostro accounts that banks hold with each other, or through local clearing systems. Third, a SWIFT payment is a chain, not a single hop. The instruction usually passes through two, three or four banks before it reaches the beneficiary. The messages that carry SWIFT payments have

entries.title: UETR Explained
entries.text: UETR Explained UETR Explained What it is The UETR Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference is a 36-character identifier that stays with a cross-border payment for its whole journey, from the ordering bank to the beneficiary bank. It is assigned once, by the bank that first instructs the payment, and it never changes. Every bank in the chain carries the same UETR in its messages about that payment, so the whole journey can be stitched together from the separate messages each bank sends. The UETR is a UUID version 4 . It has five groups of hexadecimal characters separated by hyphens, in the pattern 8-4-4-4-12. An example looks like this: 6f8e2b1a-3c4d-4e5f-9a0b-1c2d3e4f5a6b . The first group has 8 characters, then three groups of 4, then a final group of 12. The 13th character is always 4 , which marks it as a version 4 UUID, and the first character of the fourth group is 8 , 9 , a , or b , which marks the UUID variant. entries.title: ACH vs RTGS
entries.text: ACH vs RTGS ACH vs RTGS What it is ACH Automated Clearing House and RTGS Real Time Gross Settlement are two different ways of moving money between banks. They solve the same problem, getting funds from one bank account to another, but they do it in opposite ways. An ACH system collects payment instructions over a period, batches them together, nets the amounts off against each other, and settles the net result later. An RTGS system settles each payment individually, in real time, as soon as it is received. In the US, the main ACH operator is Nacha , and the main RTGS system is Fedwire , run by the Federal Reserve. In the UK, Bacs is the ACH equivalent and CHAPS is the RTGS system. In India, NEFT is a deferred net settlement system similar in spirit to ACH and RTGS is the real time gross settlement system, both run by the Reserve Bank of India. entries.title: CHAPS Explained
entries.text: CHAPS Explained CHAPS Explained What it is CHAPS Clearing House Automated Payment System is the UK's high value, same day payment system. It is a real time gross settlement system operated by the Bank of England . It is used for large payments where same day finality matters: house purchases, business to business payments, tax payments, and financial market settlements. There is no upper limit on a CHAPS payment. There is no lower limit set by the scheme, although banks typically use CHAPS for payments above 10,000 pounds because of the cost. CHAPS is operated by the Bank of England and is one of the largest high value payment systems in the world by value. Why it matters CHAPS is where the money is. Although it processes far fewer payments than Faster Payments or Bacs, the total value settled through CHAPS each day is enormous, running into hundreds of billions of pounds. A single CHAPS payment can be worth more than a whole day of Faster Payments volume. For a business analyst,

entries.title: Clearing vs Settlement
entries.text: Clearing vs Settlement Clearing vs Settlement What it is Clearing and settlement are two different stages in a payment. They are often mentioned together, but they are not the same thing, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes in payments. Clearing is the exchange, validation, and sorting of payment instructions between banks. It is the process of agreeing what is owed, to whom, and by whom. Settlement is the actual movement of funds between banks to discharge those obligations. Clearing answers the question "what do we owe each other?" Settlement answers the question "how do we pay it?" In some systems, clearing and settlement happen almost together. In others, they happen hours or days apart. Understanding the gap between them is essential for understanding payment risk, liquidity, and reconciliation. Why it matters The gap between clearing and settlement is where payment risk lives. If a bank credits a beneficiary during clearing, before settlement has happened, it

entries.title: Duplicate Payments Explained
entries.text: Duplicate Payments Explained Duplicate Payments Explained What it is A duplicate payment is a payment that is sent twice when it should have been sent once. The customer intended one payment, but the bank sent two, and the beneficiary received the money twice. The second payment is the duplicate. It is a real payment, made from the customer's account, and getting the money back requires a return or a recall. Duplicates are one of the most common payment errors, and one of the most costly. The customer loses money temporarily, the beneficiary has funds that are not theirs, and the bank has to recover the duplicate through a process that can take days. A duplicate also creates a reconciliation problem, because the customer's records show one payment and the bank's records show two. entries.title: Faster Payments Explained
entries.text: Faster Payments Explained Faster Payments Explained What it is Faster Payments is the UK's near real time payment system. It lets people and businesses send money between UK bank accounts in seconds, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It is operated by Pay.UK and is used for personal transfers, bill payments, salary payments, and business payments. The maximum value for a single Faster Payments transaction is 1 million pounds. In practice, most banks set their own lower limits for individual customers, often between 10,000 and 100,000 pounds per payment, depending on the channel and the customer. Faster Payments is not the same as CHAPS . CHAPS is the UK's high value real time gross settlement system, used for large payments such as house purchases. Faster Payments is for the high volume, lower value, near real time payments that people make every day. Why it matters Faster Payments changed what UK customers expect from a bank. entries.title: Idempotency in Payment APIs Explained
entries.text: Idempotency in Payment APIs Explained Idempotency in Payment APIs Explained What it is Idempotency means that sending the same request more than once has the same effect as sending it once. In a payment API, an idempotent request can be retried safely: if the first attempt is lost, the client can send the request again, and the payment will be made once, not twice. Without idempotency, a retry is a gamble. The client does not know whether the first request was processed, and sending it again risks paying twice. Idempotency is delivered through an idempotency key . The key is a unique value that the client generates for each logical payment, usually a UUID version 4, and sends with the payment request in a header, commonly called Idempotency-Key . The key identifies the payment request, not the payment itself. One key means one payment. entries.title: Payment APIs Explained
entries.text: Payment APIs Explained Payment APIs Explained What it is A payment API Application Programming Interface lets one system ask another system to do something with a payment, using a defined set of requests and responses over the internet. Instead of uploading a file or typing into a screen, a customer, a partner, or an internal system sends a structured request to the bank's API, and the bank responds with a structured result. Payment APIs are used for payment initiation starting a payment , status enquiry asking where a payment is , account information checking a balance or a statement , and webhooks receiving a notification when something changes . They are the foundation of open banking, of embedded finance, and of most modern fintech products. A payment API is not a single thing. It is a set of endpoints, each of which does one job, with defined request and response formats, authentication rules, and error handling. Why it matters APIs are how modern payments work. A marketplace

entries.title: Payment Exception Handling
entries.text: Payment Exception Handling Payment Exception Handling What it is Payment exception handling is the process of dealing with payments that do not complete normally. An exception is any payment that fails validation, is rejected by a clearing system, is returned, is recalled, is delayed, is duplicated, or is stuck in an unknown state. Exceptions are a normal part of payment operations. A bank that processes millions of payments a day will have thousands of exceptions. The quality of a bank's exception handling determines how quickly customers get their money back, how much manual work operations teams do, and how much the bank loses to errors. The exception lifecycle has five stages: detection finding the exception , classification understanding what type it is , investigation finding the root cause , resolution fixing it: repair, return, recall, or reverse , and prevention changing something so it does not happen again . Why it matters Exceptions are where customers form their opinion

entries.title: Payment Gateway vs Payment Hub
entries.text: Payment Gateway vs Payment Hub Payment Gateway vs Payment Hub What it is A payment gateway and a payment hub sound similar, but they solve different problems for different customers. Confusing them is one of the most common errors in payments conversations, and it leads to requirements that ask the wrong system to do the wrong job. A payment gateway is the merchant-facing front door for accepting payments. When a customer pays on a website or in an app, the gateway takes the card details, checks them, and routes the payment to the merchant's acquirer. It is built for merchants: online shops, subscription businesses, marketplaces, and apps. Examples are the checkout services offered by Stripe, Adyen, and Checkout.com. A payment hub is the bank-side central system that processes payments for the bank itself. entries.title: Payment Hub Architecture
entries.text: Payment Hub Architecture Payment Hub Architecture What it is A payment hub is the central system in a bank that receives payment instructions from all channels, validates them, enriches them, routes them to the right clearing system, and tracks them through to settlement and reconciliation. It is the single place where every payment in the bank passes through, regardless of whether it started in a mobile app, a branch, a corporate file, or an API. The hub sits between the channels where customers instruct payments and the clearing systems where payments are settled . Below the hub are the core banking system which holds the accounts , the nostro accounts which fund cross border payments , and the ledger which records everything . Around the hub are the supporting services: sanctions screening, fraud detection, liquidity management, and the exceptions function. entries.title: Payment Lifecycle Explained
entries.text: Payment Lifecycle Explained Payment Lifecycle Explained What it is The payment lifecycle is the complete journey of a payment from the moment it is instructed to the moment it is fully reconciled. It has seven distinct stages, and each stage is a separate event with its own timing, its own system, and its own risks. The stages are: 1. Initiation. The customer instructs the payment. 2. Processing. The bank validates, enriches, and routes the payment. 3. Clearing. The payment instruction is exchanged and validated between banks. 4. Settlement. Funds move between banks to discharge the obligation. 5. Beneficiary credit. The beneficiary's bank credits the beneficiary's account. 6. Ledger posting. The bank records the payment in its ledger. 7. Reconciliation. The bank matches the payment against clearing confirmations, settlement entries, and ledger postings to confirm everything agrees. These stages are not interchangeable. A payment can be initiated but not processed. It can be processed

entries.title: Payment Orchestration
entries.text: Payment Orchestration Payment Orchestration What it is Payment orchestration is the intelligent management of how a payment moves from instruction to settlement. It decides which route a payment takes, which provider or clearing system to use, what happens if the first choice fails, and how to optimise for cost, speed, and success rate. Orchestration sits above the payment hub. The hub processes the payment. The orchestrator decides the best path for it. In a simple bank, the hub has a static routing table and the payment always takes the same route. In an orchestrated setup, the route is chosen dynamically based on real time data: the cost of each route, the speed, the current success rate, the time of day, and the payment's own characteristics. Orchestration is most common in payment service providers and fintechs that route payments across multiple providers. entries.title: Payment Processing Engine Explained
entries.text: Payment Processing Engine Explained Payment Processing Engine Explained What it is A payment processing engine is the component that executes a payment: it takes an instruction, runs it through the lifecycle, and produces the result. It is the part of a payment system that actually does the work, step by step, and it is distinct from the payment hub , which is the whole system around it. Think of the hub as the building and the engine as the machinery inside it. The hub provides the channels, the connections to clearing systems, the supporting services, and the monitoring. The engine provides the state machine that moves a payment from received to settled, the validation that checks it, the ledger posting that records it, and the retry and recovery logic that handles failures. An engine can sit inside a hub, or it can stand alone. A small fintech may run a single engine that processes all its payments. entries.title: Payment Repair Explained
entries.text: Payment Repair Explained Payment Repair Explained What it is Payment repair is the manual work of fixing a payment that failed automated processing and putting it back on its journey. When a payment cannot be processed straight through, the payment hub moves it into a repair queue , where an operations analyst reviews the problem, corrects the payment, and releases it. The payment is repaired, not rejected, because the underlying instruction is usually valid. Something about the data is wrong, and a person needs to fix it. A repair queue is not a single queue. A bank typically runs several, each for a different type of problem. A data repair queue holds payments with missing or invalid fields. A compliance queue holds payments stopped by a sanctions or fraud screening hit. An account repair queue holds payments where the beneficiary account cannot be found. entries.title: Payment Routing
entries.text: Payment Routing Payment Routing What it is Payment routing is the process of deciding which path a payment takes from the sending bank to the receiving bank. The route determines which clearing system, which correspondent bank, and which settlement account are used. Routing is driven by routing tables and static data maintained by the bank's payments team. Every payment has a route. A domestic payment in the UK might route through Faster Payments or CHAPS. A euro payment might route through SEPA or SWIFT. A cross border payment might route through one correspondent bank or a chain of three. The routing decision is made by the payment hub, based on the payment's characteristics and the bank's routing rules. Why it matters Routing decides the cost, the speed, and the reliability of a payment. A payment routed through the wrong correspondent costs more and takes longer. entries.title: Payment Status State Machine Explained
entries.text: Payment Status State Machine Explained Payment Status State Machine Explained What it is A payment status state machine is the formal model of the lifecycle of a payment. It defines the states a payment can be in, the transitions that move it from one state to another, and who is allowed to make each move. Every payment in a bank follows the same state machine, from the moment it is received to the moment it reaches a final state. A typical payment state machine has these states: - Received. The payment instruction has arrived at the bank and been recorded, but no checks have run yet. - Validated. The payment has passed the bank's validation checks: the account and beneficiary details, the amount, the currency, the value date, and the sanctions and fraud screening. - Queued. The payment has passed validation and is waiting to be sent, usually because it is held for a cut-off time, a value date, or a batch. - Sent. entries.title: RTP Explained
entries.text: RTP Explained RTP Explained What it is RTP Real Time Payments is the real time payment system for the United States, operated by The Clearing House TCH . It lets banks send and receive payments in real time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with immediate confirmation and final settlement. The transaction limit for RTP is 10 million dollars. This was raised from 1 million dollars on 9 February 2025, reflecting the growing use of RTP for larger business payments. RTP is separate from FedNow , which is the Federal Reserve's real time payment system. Both are real time payment systems in the US, but they are operated by different organisations and banks may connect to one or both. Why it matters The US was late to real time payments compared to the UK, Europe, and India. RTP, launched in 2017, and FedNow, launched in 2023, changed that. Businesses can now pay suppliers instantly, workers can receive wages in real time, and consumers can send money to each other immediately, at any time.

entries.title: SEPA Explained: the Single Euro Payments Area
entries.text: SEPA Explained: the Single Euro Payments Area SEPA Explained: the Single Euro Payments Area SEPA is the set of rules that lets euro payments move between bank accounts across Europe as easily as domestic payments move inside one country. It covers 36 countries, it runs on ISO 20022 messages, and it is the default rail for euro payments for any bank operating in Europe, which is why every payments BA working on euro products needs to know its schemes, its rulebooks and its timelines. What it is SEPA Single Euro Payments Area is the system that lets euro payments move between bank accounts across Europe as easily as domestic payments move inside one country. It covers 36 countries: the 27 EU member states plus the UK, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Switzerland, Monaco, San Marino, Andorra, and Vatican City. SEPA has two main instruments. SCT SEPA Credit Transfer moves money from a payer to a payee. SDD SEPA Direct Debit lets a payee pull money from a payer's account with a mandate.

entries.title: SEPA Instant Explained
entries.text: SEPA Instant Explained SEPA Instant Explained What it is SEPA Instant Credit Transfer SCT Inst is the instant payment scheme for euro payments. A payment instructed under SCT Inst must reach the payee's bank within 10 seconds, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. There is no cut-off, no business day, and no waiting until morning. SCT Inst is governed by a rulebook from the European Payments Council EPC . The settlement happens through TIPS TARGET Instant Payment Settlement , the Eurosystem's instant settlement service, or through other clearing and settlement mechanisms that support instant payments. The Instant Payments Regulation, Regulation EU 2024/886 , makes instant payments mandatory for banks in the euro area. It also makes Verification of Payee VoP mandatory, so the payer is shown the name matching the account before the payment is sent. The SCT Inst amount cap was removed by the 2025 rulebook. entries.title: Straight-Through Processing (STP) Explained
entries.text: Straight-Through Processing (STP) Explained Straight-Through Processing STP Explained What it is Straight-through processing , or STP , means a payment is processed from instruction to settlement without any manual intervention. The payment is received, validated, screened, routed, and sent by systems, with no person touching it at any point. A payment that goes straight through is faster, cheaper, and less likely to go wrong than a payment that stops for manual work. The STP rate is the share of payments that go straight through. It is calculated as the number of payments processed with no manual intervention, divided by the total number of payments, expressed as a percentage. A bank that processes 10,000 payments in a day and repairs 800 of them has an STP rate of 92 percent. The other 8 percent went to a repair queue, a compliance review, or an exception. entries.title: TARGET Services Explained: How Euro Payments Settle in Central Bank Money
entries.text: TARGET Services Explained: How Euro Payments Settle in Central Bank Money TARGET Services Explained: How Euro Payments Settle in Central Bank Money TARGET Services are the Eurosystem's market infrastructure services, and they are where euro payments actually settle. T2 settles large-value euro payments, TIPS settles instant payments, T2S settles securities trades, and ECMS manages the collateral behind them, all in central bank money, which is the safest form of settlement there is. What it is TARGET Services are the Eurosystem's market infrastructure services: the systems that settle payments, securities, and collateral in central bank money in the euro area. The Eurosystem is the European Central Bank plus the national central banks of the countries that use the euro. TARGET Services are operated by the Eurosystem, and they are the backbone of the euro payment system. There are four TARGET Services. entries.title: UPI Explained: India's Unified Payments Interface
entries.text: UPI Explained: India's Unified Payments Interface UPI Explained: India's Unified Payments Interface UPI is India's real time payment system for person to person and person to merchant payments. It lets anyone with a bank account and a mobile phone send and receive money instantly, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, using a Virtual Payment Address instead of an account number, and it is the largest real time payment system in the world by volume. What it is UPI Unified Payments Interface is India's real time payment system for person to person and person to merchant payments. It is operated by the National Payments Corporation of India NPCI . It lets anyone with a bank account and a mobile phone send and receive money instantly, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, using a mobile app. UPI works through a Virtual Payment Address VPA , such as name@bankname, so people do not need to share their account number and IFSC code. entries.title: Write Requirements for Same-Day Cross-Border Payments for SMEs
entries.text: Write Requirements for Same-Day Cross-Border Payments for SMEs Requirement analysis A mid-sized bank wants to offer same-day cross-border payments to its small and medium enterprise customers, who today wait two to three days for supplier payments to arrive. The current process relies on manual checks, emailed instructions and a correspondent chain that the customer cannot track. In this lab you act as the business analyst who turns that business problem into a clear, testable set of requirements. You will define the objectives and the scope, identify the stakeholders, record the assumptions and dependencies, and write the business rules that govern cutoffs, charges and value dates. You will then separate functional requirements from non-functional requirements, so that the development team knows what the solution must do and how well it must do it. By the end of the lab you will have a requirements pack that a sponsor can sign off and a development team can build from without

entries.title: Redesign the Payment Exception Repair Process
entries.text: Redesign the Payment Exception Repair Process Process modelling When a payment cannot be processed straight through, it lands in an exception queue where operations staff must repair it, return it or reject it. In many banks that queue is slow, opaque and full of rework, because nobody has mapped the process end to end. In this lab you model the as-is exception repair process, measure where time is lost, and design a to-be process that clears most exceptions on first touch. You will draw a BPMN diagram with clear swimlanes, add sequence diagrams for the system interactions, and model the exception flows for the most common failure types. You will also define the controls, the handoffs and the service levels for each step. By the end of the lab you will have a process design that operations can run, technology can build, and management can measure. entries.title: Map MT103 to pacs.008 for a Migration
entries.text: Map MT103 to pacs.008 for a Migration Data and messaging Migrating from MT103 to pacs.008 is a data exercise before it is a technology exercise, and the quality of the mapping decides whether payments arrive intact. In this lab you build a source-to-target mapping for a real migration scope, starting from a canonical data model and working down to field level rules. You will decide which fields are mandatory, optional or defaulted, write the transformation rules for party data, addresses, remittance information and charges, and define the validation rules that catch bad data before it leaves the bank. You will also record data lineage, so that any field in the outgoing pacs.008 can be traced back to its source. By the end of the lab you will have a mapping sheet that developers can build from and testers can verify against. entries.title: Specify a Payment Initiation API for a Corporate Channel
entries.text: Specify a Payment Initiation API for a Corporate Channel API analysis A corporate banking channel needs an API that lets treasury systems initiate payments directly, without a person typing each instruction into a screen. The API must be easy to integrate, safe against duplicate payments, and clear about what went wrong when a request fails. In this lab you analyse and specify a payment initiation API from the business need down to the contract. You will define the endpoints, the HTTP methods, the request and response schemas, the authentication model, the error codes, and the rules for idempotency, correlation IDs, timeouts and retries. You will also write the OpenAPI contract that the corporate integration team builds against. By the end of the lab you will have an API specification that is complete enough to hand to a developer and a corporate customer without a follow-up meeting. entries.title: Deliver an Instant Payments Feature in Three Sprints
entries.text: Deliver an Instant Payments Feature in Three Sprints Agile delivery An instant payments feature must reach customers in weeks, not months, and the work must be split into pieces that a team can build, test and release in short sprints. In this lab you plan and run the delivery of an instant payments feature across three two-week sprints. You will break an epic into features and user stories, write acceptance criteria in plain language and in Gherkin, build and prioritise the backlog, and plan the sprint goals, the stand-ups, the reviews and the retrospectives. You will also define the RACI for the release and the definition of done that decides when a story is truly finished. By the end of the lab you will have a delivery plan that a product owner, a scrum master and a development team can execute together. entries.title: Write a UAT Plan for a Payment Hub Go-Live
entries.text: Write a UAT Plan for a Payment Hub Go-Live Testing A payment hub go-live is a moment when a testing gap becomes a customer problem within minutes, so the user acceptance test must be thorough, realistic and well organised. In this lab you write the UAT plan for a payment hub go-live, covering system integration testing, user acceptance testing, reconciliation and production validation. You will design happy path, negative, boundary, integration and regression scenarios, plan the defect triage process, and define the entry and exit criteria that decide whether the hub is ready. You will also prepare the reconciliation checks that prove every payment reached the right ledger. By the end of the lab you will have a test plan that the business can sign off with confidence and the test team can execute without improvisation. entries.title: Deliver a Cross-Border Correspondent Payment in US Dollars
entries.text: Deliver a Cross-Border Correspondent Payment in US Dollars Cross-border correspondent payment A corporate customer in London needs to pay a supplier in New York in US dollars, and the bank must move the money through correspondent banks, apply the agreed foreign exchange rate, deduct the correct charges, and settle on the agreed value date. Today the process depends on manual checks, emailed instructions, and a chain of intermediaries that the customer cannot see, so payments are slow, expensive, and hard to explain when they arrive late or short. In this lab you act as the business analyst for the full flow. You will compare the serial method, where the payment instruction travels with the funds through each correspondent, with the cover method, where the instruction travels directly and the funds settle separately. entries.title: Deliver an Instant Payment with Timeout and Duplicate Controls
entries.text: Deliver an Instant Payment with Timeout and Duplicate Controls Instant payment A retail customer sends money from a mobile app and expects it to arrive in seconds, at any hour, with a clear confirmation on screen. Behind that simple tap sits a tight chain: real time validation of the account, the limits, and the funds, sanctions screening in seconds, a liquidity check, settlement with the clearing system, and a confirmation back to the sender. If any link is slow, the payment must time out safely, and if the customer taps twice, the payment must never be sent twice. In this lab you act as the business analyst for the full instant payment flow. You will define the validation rules, the timeout limits, the duplicate prevention controls, the settlement steps, and the confirmation and failure messages. entries.title: Deliver a Card Payment from Authorisation to Dispute
entries.text: Deliver a Card Payment from Authorisation to Dispute Card payment A customer pays with a card in a shop or online, and the money must move through authorisation, clearing, settlement, and reconciliation, with refunds and disputes handled fairly when things go wrong. The shop needs a fast answer at the till, the cardholder needs a clear statement, the merchant needs to be paid on time, and the bank needs to match every transaction to its ledger. entries.text: Reconcile Payments Across Messages, Statements, and Ledger Payment reconciliation Every payment leaves a trail in several places: the payment message, the nostro statement, the clearing record, the settlement record, and the ledger. entries.title: What is a payment?
entries.text: A payment is the transfer of value from one party to another in order to settle an obligation. When you buy a coffee, pay rent, send a salary, or settle a supplier invoice, you are making a payment. The obligation can come from a purchase, a loan, a tax, a salary agreement, or any commitment where one party owes value to another. The payment discharges that obligation, fully or partly, and creates a record that the debt has been reduced or cleared. In a modern banking context, a payment almost always involves accounts held with regulated institutions and a set of instructions that tell those institutions what to move, from whom, to whom, and for what reason. The instructions travel as a payment message, while the actual value moves through accounts and settlement systems. A payment can be

entries.title: What is a payment rail?
entries.text: A payment rail is the infrastructure that carries a payment from one party to another. Think of it like a railway track. The train is the payment instruction, and the rail is the set of systems, rules, and connections that let the train reach its destination safely. A rail includes the network that moves the message, the clearing system that exchanges instructions between banks, the settlement system that moves value between banks, and the scheme rules that define cut off times, value dates, and liability when something goes wrong. Common examples help make this concrete. In India, UPI, IMPS, NEFT, and RTGS are different rails with different speeds, limits, and settlement models. entries.title: What is the difference between a payment instruction and settlement? Why does the distinction matter in system design?
entries.text: The payment instruction is the **pacs.008** or the **pain.001** that tells the bank to move money. Settlement is the actual movement of funds between banks that discharges the obligation. They are different events and they can happen at different times. When a customer submits a payment, the hub creates a pacs.008 and sends it through the clearing system. The clearing system processes it and returns a **pacs.002** with a status. When the status is ACSC, settlement has happened. Until then, the payment is only an instruction. The gap matters because a payment can be instructed but not settled, for example if the clearing house rejects it, or if the settlement account has insufficient funds. The bank must track both states separately. The **instruction status** tells the customer what

entries.title: What is the difference between a branch, a subsidiary and an entity in payment routing?
entries.text: These three words describe different legal structures, and they change how a payment moves. A branch is part of the same legal entity as the head office. A London bank with a branch in Singapore is one legal entity, so money moving between London and Singapore is an internal transfer, not a payment between two banks. A subsidiary is a separate legal entity owned by the parent bank. A UK bank with a subsidiary in India is two legal entities, so a payment between them is a real payment that must go through proper channels and be recorded as an intercompany transaction. An entity is the general word for a legal unit of the bank, and a large bank can have hundreds of entities across different countries. entries.title: What is a payment factory model and why do large banks use it?
entries.text: A payment factory is a model where a large bank centralises all payment processing into one shared service instead of letting each business unit run its own payments. In a bank like JP Morgan, the corporate banking team, the retail team and the private banking team all send their payment instructions to the same factory. The factory handles validation, routing, clearing and exceptions the same way for everyone. The benefit is scale and consistency. One team maintains the payment logic, one set of controls applies to all payments, and a change to a regulation is made once, not in five different systems. The factory also gives the bank a single view of all payment volumes, which helps treasury manage liquidity and helps risk manage exposure. The challenge is that different business units

entries.title: How does a bank join a clearing system as a direct participant versus using an indirect clearer? What changes operationally?
entries.text: A **direct participant** connects to the clearing system itself, holds a **settlement account** at the central bank, and settles its own payments. The bank must meet the clearing system's technical, financial, and operational requirements, hold enough collateral, and staff an operations team that can manage the connection, the queue, and the settlement account through the day. The bank has full control over its payments, its cut-off management, and its liquidity. An **indirect participant** uses a direct participant, called a clearer, to settle on its behalf. The bank sends its payments to the clearer, and the clearer settles them through its own central bank account. entries.title: What is straight-through processing and what breaks it?
entries.text: Straight-through processing, or STP, means a payment goes from instruction to settlement without any human touching it. The instruction arrives, the system validates it, routes it, sends it to clearing and confirms settlement, all automatically. STP is the goal for large banks because it is fast, cheap and consistent. A bank like Standard Chartered aims for a high STP rate, often above 95 percent for standard payments. What breaks STP is anything that needs a human decision. A missing field, for example a beneficiary name that does not match the account, stops the payment. A sanctions hit stops it. A payment above a limit needs manual approval. entries.title: What is straight through processing, and how do you design a payment system to maximise it? What is a realistic STP rate?
entries.text: Straight through processing means a payment goes from initiation to settlement without any manual touch. To design for it, you need four things. First, **complete data at initiation**. The channel must capture every mandatory field before the payment is accepted, so nothing is missing downstream. Second, **automated validation**. The hub checks the account, the balance, the sanctions lists and the message format without human help. Third, **clean routing rules**. The hub decides the clearing system, the settlement method and the charge option from static data, not from someone reading the payment. entries.title: Walk me through a clean domestic credit transfer end to end, from the customer submitting the instruction to the beneficiary being credited. What does each stage look like when nothing goes wrong?
entries.text: A clean domestic credit transfer has five stages, and in a good flow none of them needs a human hand. First the customer submits the instruction, usually from a mobile app or corporate channel, as a **pain.001** message. The bank validates it immediately, checking the account, the balance, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists, and answers with a **pain.002** acceptance. Second, the payment engine builds the interbank message, a **pacs.008** for a credit transfer, and routes it to the domestic clearing system. Third, the clearing system settles it, moving funds between the banks through their settlement accounts. Fourth, the beneficiary bank receives the **pacs.008**, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, which means settlement complete.

entries.text: Straight through processing means a payment flows from initiation to settlement with no manual intervention. The customer submits the instruction through a channel, and the payment hub validates it automatically. The validation checks the account number format, the balance, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists, all in milliseconds. The hub enriches the payment, adding the routing details, the value date, and the settlement method from **static data**. It converts the instruction into the right interbank format, a **pacs.008** for a customer credit transfer, and sends it to the clearing system. entries.title: A customer sends a payment and receives an ACSC confirmation within minutes. What does ACSC mean, and why does a fast confirmation matter?
entries.text: A prompt ACSC confirmation means the payment settled, and it matters because it closes the loop for the customer. The sending bank sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system. The clearing system settles it and the beneficiary bank credits the account. The beneficiary bank sends back a **pacs.002** with **ACSC status**, which means accepted, settled, and credited. The sending bank receives the ACSC, updates the payment status, and tells the customer the payment has arrived. The customer sees the confirmation in their app or receives a notification, and they can tell their supplier the money is there. entries.title: What is Fedwire?
entries.text: Fedwire is the United States real time gross settlement system operated by the Federal Reserve. It is the system through which banks settle large value payments in central bank money, one transaction at a time, with immediate finality. When a bank sends a payment through Fedwire, the Federal Reserve debits the sending bank master account and credits the receiving bank master account, and the payment is final at that moment. There is no netting and no waiting for an end of day batch. Fedwire is used for high value and time critical payments: interbank transfers, settlement of securities transactions, corporate treasury payments, and large customer payments where certainty matters. entries.title: What is CHIPS?
entries.text: CHIPS, the Clearing House Interbank Payments System, is a private sector US payment system operated by The Clearing House, and it is the main system for large value US dollar payments. It is used heavily for international payments: when a bank outside the US sends dollars to a bank inside the US, the payment very often clears through CHIPS. It also handles domestic large value transfers between US banks. CHIPS is a net settlement system, which is its defining difference from Fedwire. In CHIPS, payments are not settled one by one in central bank money as they arrive. Instead, they are queued, offset against each other where possible, and settled on a net basis through a prefunded account at the Federal Reserve. entries.title: What is Faster Payments (UK)?
entries.text: Faster Payments is the United Kingdom real time payment system, launched in 2008 and operated by Pay.UK. It lets people and businesses send sterling payments between UK bank accounts in seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. It is the system behind most everyday instant payments in the UK: paying a friend, paying a bill, or a business paying a supplier. When you make an instant transfer from your UK banking app, it is almost certainly travelling over Faster Payments. The system works through participating banks and payment service providers. The payer bank sends the payment instruction, the system validates and routes it, the beneficiary bank credits the account and confirms, and the payer sees the result within seconds. entries.title: What is CHAPS?
entries.text: CHAPS, the Clearing House Automated Payment System, is the United Kingdom high value payment system, operated by the Bank of England. It is the UK equivalent of Fedwire: a real time gross settlement system in which each payment is settled individually and immediately in central bank money, with finality at the moment of settlement. It is used for payments where value, certainty and timing matter most, such as house purchases, large corporate payments, and settlement between financial institutions. A CHAPS payment is typically high value, and there is no upper limit in principle, although banks set their own limits and charges. entries.title: What is RTGS?
entries.text: RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement. It is a system in which each payment is settled individually, in real time, in central bank money, as soon as it is submitted and validated. There is no batching and no netting: every payment is processed on its own, and the funds move from the sending bank's account at the central bank to the receiving bank's account immediately. The word gross is important. It means each payment is settled for its full value, not netted against other payments. If a bank sends ten payments of 10 lakh rupees each, RTGS settles ten separate transfers of 10 lakh rupees.
