entries.title: What is RTGS in India and what is the minimum amount?
entries.text: RTGS, the Real Time Gross Settlement system, is India's high value payment system operated by the Reserve Bank of India. It settles each transaction individually and in real time, rather than netting transactions together in a batch. The word gross means each payment is settled for its full amount, one by one, in central bank money. RTGS is designed for large value, time critical payments such as interbank transfers, government securities settlements, and large corporate payments. The minimum amount for an RTGS transaction is 2 lakh rupees. There is no maximum amount, so transactions worth crores of rupees can be settled through RTGS. RTGS operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, including holidays, since December 2020. Before that, it operated only during banking hours. A customer

entries.title: A corporate client needs to send a £250,000 payment to a supplier in the UK today. How do you decide between CHAPS and Faster Payments, and what happens step by step once you choose?
entries.text: The first check is the amount and the value date. **Faster Payments** has a per-transaction limit that varies by bank, usually around £250,000 to £1 million, and it settles in seconds. **CHAPS** has no upper limit and settles in central bank money on the same day, but it costs more and runs to a cut-off, usually around 5 PM. For £250,000 the bank checks its own Faster Payments limit first. If the payment fits, Faster Payments is the default because it is cheaper and instant for the customer. If it exceeds the limit, or the client needs the certainty of central bank settlement, the bank uses CHAPS. Once the route is chosen, the **payment hub** builds the instruction and sends it to the clearing system. For CHAPS, the hub sends the payment to the **Bank of England RTGS** system, where it

entries.title: A corporate client submits a payment at 4:45 PM for same-day settlement through CHAPS. The CHAPS cut-off is 5 PM. Walk me through what happens if the payment misses the cut-off.
entries.text: The cut-off is a hard deadline set by the clearing system, not by the bank. If the instruction reaches the **Bank of England RTGS** after the cut-off, it is rejected for same-day settlement. The bank cannot force it through. The first thing the **payment hub** does is check the status. If the payment was submitted before the cut-off but is still being processed, the hub tries to release it in time. If it misses, the payment is not lost, but the value date moves to the next working day. The bank then has three jobs. First, update the payment status in the hub and the channel so the client can see the new value date. Second, tell the client proactively, because a missed value date can break a supplier contract or a property completion. Third, decide with the client whether to hold the

entries.title: How does Faster Payments settle between banks if the customer sees the money instantly? Explain the deferred net settlement behind it.
entries.text: The customer experience and the bank-to-bank settlement are two different things. When a customer sends a **Faster Payment**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer within seconds. That is the customer leg, and it is instant. But the banks do not settle with each other at that moment. Instead, Faster Payments uses **deferred net settlement**. Each bank's payments are recorded through the day, and at set times, usually three times a day, the central system nets all the payments between each pair of banks and settles only the net amount. This means the beneficiary bank is taking a risk. It has credited its customer before it has received the funds from the sending bank. The risk is managed in two ways. First, each bank must hold collateral and prefund a settlement account, so there is

entries.title: A Fedwire payment is sent in the US. How does Fedwire settle, and how is it different from CHIPS?
entries.text: **Fedwire** is the **Federal Reserve's** real-time gross settlement system. Each payment settles individually, in central bank money, the moment it is sent. The sending bank's **Federal Reserve account** is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited immediately. There is no netting and no delay. Fedwire is used for high-value, time-critical payments, and it is final the moment it settles. If the sending bank does not have enough balance, the payment queues, and the bank can use the Federal Reserve's intraday credit facility. **CHIPS** is different. It is a private-sector clearing house run by **The Clearing House**. CHIPS uses a hybrid model. Payments are queued and settled through a combination of real-time settlement and multilateral netting. Banks prefund a CHIPS account, and

entries.title: The bank sends a payment through CHIPS for a US dollar payment. How does CHIPS net settlement work, and what happens if a bank fails to fund its position?
entries.text: **CHIPS** settles US dollar payments through a combination of real-time settlement and multilateral netting. Each participating bank prefunds a **CHIPS account** at the start of the day. When a bank sends a payment, CHIPS checks whether the payment can settle immediately from the prefunded balance, or whether it should wait in the queue until incoming payments from other banks create enough offset. The system continuously looks for groups of queued payments that can be settled together by netting them, so each bank only funds the net amount, not the gross. If a bank fails to fund its net position, the system cannot settle its outgoing payments. CHIPS will hold those payments in the queue and try again as more funds arrive. If the shortfall persists, the bank must add funds to its CHIPS

entries.title: Walk through a clean Faster Payments transfer in the UK. How does a payment move from one bank account to another in seconds?
entries.text: Faster Payments works because it is built for speed. The customer sends a payment from their mobile app, and the sending bank validates it in real time, checking the sort code, the account number, and the balance. The bank sends the payment to the **Faster Payments** central infrastructure, which routes it to the beneficiary bank in seconds. The beneficiary bank credits the customer account almost immediately and sends back a confirmation. The whole flow takes seconds, not hours. The limits are clear, a maximum amount per payment and a maximum per day, and the bank tells the customer these limits upfront. The payment is **irrevocable** once sent, so the customer must check the details before confirming. The sending bank receives a confirmation that the payment was accepted, and the

entries.title: Walk through a clean CHAPS payment. How does a high-value same-day payment settle through the Bank of England?
entries.text: CHAPS is the UK high-value same-day system, and it works because settlement is real time and final. The corporate customer submits the instruction before the CHAPS **cut-off**, usually through a corporate channel. The bank validates it, runs sanctions screening, and applies the **four-eyes approval** for high-value amounts. The payment hub sends the **pacs.008** to the Bank of England, which operates CHAPS. The Bank of England moves the funds between the banks settlement accounts immediately, and the payment is **final and irrevocable** the moment it settles. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the customer account the same day, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. The customer gets confirmation the same day, and the end-of-day **camt.053** shows the debit.

entries.title: Walk through a clean Fedwire payment in the US. How does a high-value USD payment settle in real time through the Federal Reserve?
entries.text: Fedwire is the US high-value real-time system, and it works because the Federal Reserve settles each payment individually and immediately. The customer submits the instruction, and the bank validates it, checking the **ABA routing number**, the account, the balance, and the sanctions lists. The bank sends the payment to the **Federal Reserve**, which debits the sending bank's reserve account and credits the receiving bank's reserve account in real time. The payment is final the moment the Fed processes it. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the customer account, and the customer sees the funds the same day. The sending bank gets a confirmation, and the end-of-day statement shows the debit. For a cross-border payment, the US leg works the same way. A payment from overseas

entries.title: Walk through a clean direct debit collection, from the mandate to the debit to the biller being credited. How does the scheme protect the customer?
entries.text: A clean direct debit starts with a **mandate**. The customer authorises the biller to collect payments from their account, and the mandate is stored by the bank. On the collection date, the biller sends the collection instruction to their bank. The biller bank sends a **pain.008** to the debtor bank, carrying the mandate reference, the amount, and the collection date. The debtor bank checks the mandate, checks the balance, and debits the customer account. The funds move to the biller bank, which credits the biller account. The customer sees the debit in their statement, and the biller sees the credit. If the customer disputes the collection, they can request a **refund** within the scheme rules, and the bank processes it through a pacs.004 return. The scheme gives the customer strong

entries.title: What is a nostro FX conversion?
entries.text: A nostro FX conversion is a currency conversion that a bank performs using the funds held in its own nostro account, rather than buying the currency in the market at the moment of the payment. For example, if BNP Paribas holds US dollars in its nostro account with Wells Fargo, and it needs to pay USD 367,574.90 to Banco Santander, it can use the dollars already in the account, with no FX trade needed. If instead it holds only euros in Paris and needs to pay dollars, it must sell euros and buy dollars, and that trade is settled by delivering dollars into the Wells Fargo nostro account. The conversion rate is the rate agreed for that trade, and the dollars are then available for the payment. Nostro FX conversions are managed by the treasury team, which watches the balance in each currency

entries.title: A payment starts at a branch in London and ends at a beneficiary in Singapore. Walk me through the hops inside the bank.
entries.text: The customer gives the instruction at the branch, and the branch system sends it to the payment hub. The hub validates the instruction, checks the account balance and screens it for sanctions. Next the hub decides the route. For Singapore the payment will usually go through the bank's own network if it has a Singapore entity, or through a correspondent bank. The hub creates an ISO 20022 message, a pacs.008, and sends it to the Singapore entity or the correspondent. If the bank has its own Singapore branch, the payment moves internally. The London hub debits the customer's account, and the Singapore entity credits the beneficiary. The two entities settle between themselves through their internal accounts. If a correspondent is used, the payment goes over SWIFT to the correspondent bank,

entries.title: A company in India pays a supplier in Germany 250,000 euro through a pain.001. The sending bank transmits the pacs.008, but the beneficiary bank flags a name mismatch and the funds sit uncredited for three days. How do you resolve it?
entries.text: I read the **pacs.002** first. A status of Pending means the beneficiary bank is holding the payment, not rejecting it. That distinction matters, because a held payment can still be credited once the issue is resolved. I raise a **camt.029 investigation query** to get the exact mismatch detail from the beneficiary bank, because I need to know precisely which part of the name differs. Then I work the exception with the intermediary and the beneficiary bank, confirming the correct beneficiary name with the sender. If the name is **corrected and verified**, the bank applies the funds to the account and the payment completes. If it cannot be resolved, the payment comes back through a **pacs.004**. Throughout the three days I keep the corporate customer informed, because days of silence are

entries.title: A cross border payment was processed with the wrong FX rate. The customer received less than they should have. How do you investigate and fix it?
entries.text: The first step is to find the **source of truth** for the FX rate. In a bank, the treasury system publishes rates, and the payment hub must use the same rate the customer was quoted. If the hub used a different rate, the customer was overcharged or undercharged. Check the **rate timestamp** on the payment record and compare it against the treasury rate at that moment. Then check the **rate type**. A customer rate includes a margin, a wholesale rate does not, and mixing them up is a common error. Next, check the **currency pair direction**. EUR to USD is not the same as USD to EUR, and inverting the pair is a classic mapping bug. Also check whether the payment went through an **intermediary currency**. Some corridors convert EUR to USD to INR, and each leg applies its own rate. If the hub

entries.title: Walk me through a clean cross-border payment end to end, from the corporate customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. How do the instruction and the money move together?
entries.text: A clean cross-border payment has two parallel tracks, the instruction track and the money track, and both must complete for the payment to land. The corporate customer sends a **pain.001** to their bank. The bank validates it, checks sanctions, checks the balance, and sends a **pain.002** acceptance. The bank then sends a **pacs.008** instruction to the beneficiary bank, carrying the full customer and remittance details. At the same time, the funds move through the correspondent chain. If the cover method is used, a **pacs.009** with settlement method COVE moves the money between correspondents through their **Nostro accounts**. Each hop sends back a **pacs.002** status, ACTC when accepted, ACSP when processing, and ACSC when settled. The beneficiary bank receives both the instruction and

entries.title: Walk through a clean FX conversion on a cross-border payment. How does the rate get locked and the beneficiary receive exactly the quoted amount?
entries.text: A clean FX conversion starts with the **rate being locked** at the moment the customer confirms the payment. The customer sees the rate, the amount in the source currency, and the amount in the target currency, and agrees. The bank executes the FX trade immediately, buying the target currency at the locked rate. The payment hub then sends the **pacs.008** in the target currency to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank credits the account in the target currency, and the customer receives exactly the amount that was quoted. The bank sends a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, and the end-of-day **camt.053** shows the debit in the source currency and the FX trade. The keys to making it clean are a **transparent rate**, so the customer knows what they are getting, a **locked rate**, so the

entries.title: What is SWIFT?
entries.text: SWIFT is the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication. It is a global messaging network used by banks and financial institutions to send secure instructions and information to each other. When a bank in India needs to tell a bank in the United Kingdom to pay a beneficiary, it often sends that instruction over SWIFT. More than 11,000 institutions in over 200 countries are connected, and they exchange millions of messages every day, covering customer payments, bank to bank transfers, trade finance, securities, and treasury operations. The most important fact about SWIFT, and the one beginners most often get wrong, is that SWIFT is a messaging system, not a payment system. It carries instructions, not money. It holds no accounts and it settles nothing. When a bank sends an

entries.title: What is SWIFT gpi?
entries.text: SWIFT gpi is the Global Payments Innovation initiative, a service that makes cross border payments faster, more transparent, and more traceable. Before gpi, a cross border payment could take several days, the customer had no idea where the money was, and the final amount was uncertain because each intermediary could deduct charges without warning. Gpi was built to fix those three problems by setting service level rules for member banks, requiring same day processing, end to end tracking, and transparency on fees and foreign exchange. The core of gpi is the tracker. Every gpi payment carries a Unique End to End Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, which stays with the payment from the debtor agent to the creditor agent. Each bank in the chain confirms when it received the payment,

entries.title: What is a nostro account?
entries.text: A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with a foreign bank, in the foreign bank's currency. The word nostro is Latin for ours, and it is used from the perspective of the bank that owns the account. So if an Indian bank holds a US dollar account with a bank in New York, the Indian bank calls that account its nostro account. The purpose of a nostro account is to make payments in that foreign currency. When the Indian bank's customer pays a supplier in the United States, the Indian bank instructs its New York correspondent to debit its nostro account and pay the beneficiary. The nostro account is prefunded, meaning the Indian bank keeps a balance there so payments can go out immediately without waiting for funds to arrive. Managing nostro accounts is a real operational task. A bank

entries.title: What is a payment versus a cover in correspondent banking?
entries.text: The serial and cover methods below are shown in their pre-migration MT form, because that form shows each method most clearly. Since coexistence ended on 22 November 2025, the same payment travels as a pacs.008 in serial, and as a pacs.008 plus a pacs.009 COV in cover. In correspondent banking, the payment and the cover are two different messages that together move money across borders, and the distinction matters most in the serial and cover methods. The payment message, usually an MT103, carries the full payment details to the beneficiary bank, including the debtor, the creditor, the amount, and the remittance information. The cover message, usually an MT202 COV, carries only the settlement instruction between banks, telling the correspondent how to move the funds to cover the payment.

entries.title: What is a nostro fee?
entries.text: A nostro fee is any charge a correspondent bank levies for holding and operating a nostro account on behalf of another bank. The most common nostro fees are a monthly account maintenance fee, a per transaction fee for each payment or receipt processed through the account, a fee for statements and reporting, and a fee for investigations or repairs. The correspondent may also charge for liquidity services, such as an overdraft facility, and for FX conversion when it converts funds in the account. Nostro fees are set out in the account tariff agreed when the account is opened, and they are usually billed monthly. The account holder can pay the invoice by a separate payment, or authorise the correspondent to debit the nostro account directly. In practice, many nostro fees are small in

entries.title: What is SWIFT gpi in detail?
entries.text: SWIFT gpi, or Global Payments Innovation, is a service launched by SWIFT in 2017 to make cross border payments faster, more transparent, and easier to track. Before gpi, a sender had no way to know where a payment was, how much had been deducted, or when it would arrive. Gpi changes that by giving every payment a unique end to end transaction reference, the UETR, and by requiring every gpi bank in the chain to confirm receipt, to confirm credit, and to report any charges deducted. The payment is tracked from the sender bank to the beneficiary bank, and the sender can see each step, including the time each bank received the payment and the amount it passed on. Gpi also sets service level agreements, so banks must confirm credit within a set time, and it provides a case resolution service

entries.title: What is gpi Case Resolution?
entries.text: Gpi Case Resolution is the SWIFT gpi service that helps banks solve problems with a gpi payment quickly, by giving them a shared case file linked to the payment UETR. When a payment is delayed, missing, or incorrect, the sender bank can open a case in the gpi Tracker, and it can send a message to the bank that currently holds the payment, asking for an update. The receiving bank must respond within the gpi SLA, and all messages in the case are stored in one place, so no one has to search through emails or phone notes. The case can cover many issues, including a payment that has not been credited, a wrong amount, a missing beneficiary, or a request for a refund. Case Resolution replaces the old MT195 and MT196 investigation messages for gpi payments, although banks can still use those

entries.title: What is a nostro account and how does a bank use it day to day?
entries.text: A nostro account is an account a bank holds with another bank in a foreign currency. For example, a UK bank like Standard Chartered holds a US dollar nostro account with a bank in New York. When the UK bank needs to pay US dollars to a beneficiary, it instructs its nostro agent in New York to pay from that account. The nostro account is funded in advance, so the bank has to predict how much it will need each day. Treasury manages this. Every morning treasury looks at the expected payment volumes, the balance in each nostro account and the funding needed. During the day, payments draw the balance down. If the balance runs low, treasury tops it up by buying dollars or moving funds. At end of day the bank reconciles the nostro account against its own ledger. Any difference is an exception

entries.title: How do correspondent banks work together on a cross-border payment?
entries.text: A cross-border payment usually passes through more than one bank because no single bank has a presence in every country. The sending bank, for example a UK bank, sends the payment to its correspondent bank in the destination country. The correspondent is a bank that has agreed to process payments on behalf of the sending bank. The sending bank holds a nostro account with the correspondent, and the correspondent debits that account when it pays the beneficiary. If the beneficiary's bank is different from the correspondent, the payment hops again to the beneficiary's bank through the local clearing system. Each bank in the chain checks the payment, screens it and takes its fee if the charge option allows it. The payment message, usually a pacs.008, travels with the payment and carries the

entries.title: A payment is sent through SWIFT to a correspondent bank. Explain the difference between the cover method and the serial method, and when you would use each.
entries.text: In the **serial method**, the payment instruction travels from bank to bank along the whole chain. Each bank in the chain receives the **MT103** or **pacs.008**, checks it, and passes it to the next bank, until it reaches the beneficiary bank. The funds move with the instruction at each hop. This works well when the banks in the chain have direct relationships and the payment is straightforward. In the **cover method**, the instruction and the funds travel separately. The ordering bank sends the payment instruction directly to the beneficiary bank, usually as an **MT103** or **pacs.008**, and separately sends a **cover payment**, an **MT202** or **pacs.009**, through the correspondent chain to fund it. The beneficiary bank credits the customer when it receives the instruction, and the

entries.title: Your bank uses SWIFT gpi. How does the gpi tracker know where a payment is, and what does the bank do when the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary?
entries.text: **SWIFT gpi** gives the bank a tracker that shows where a payment is at each step. Every bank in the chain updates the tracker when it receives and forwards the payment, and the tracker shows the status, the fees deducted, and the time at each hop. When the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary, the first step is to check the **UETR** and confirm the payment is genuinely stuck, not just slow. Some intermediaries take longer, especially if they run batch processing. If the payment is genuinely stuck, the bank contacts the intermediary directly, usually through a **SWIFT** message or a phone call to their operations team, and asks for the status. The bank also checks whether the payment failed a compliance screen at the intermediary, which is a common reason for a hold. The

entries.title: A payment used the cover method. The pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover have both settled, and now the customer payment needs to be returned. How do you unwind the cover leg?
entries.text: The cover is a separate settlement, so it gets a separate return. Returning the customer payment does not automatically unwind the cover. I recognise the two legs. The **pacs.008 instruction** travelled to the beneficiary bank, while the **pacs.009 with settlement method COVE** settled the funds between correspondents. To return the payment, I need a **pacs.004** for the customer leg and a separate pacs.004 for the cover leg. I match each return to its original using the **UETR and settlement references**, so nothing gets misapplied. I watch for partial amounts, because the cover returned may differ from the cover sent if charges were taken along the way. Both the original cover and its return hit the **Nostro ledger**, so both must be booked and reconciled. Reconciliation must pair all

entries.title: What is a nostro account, and how does the payment hub interact with it? What happens if the nostro balance is too low?
entries.text: A **nostro account** is your bank's account with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency. When you send a USD payment from India, your bank debits the customer's INR account, converts to USD, and then instructs its correspondent bank in the US to pay from the nostro account. The nostro balance goes down. When you receive a USD payment, the correspondent credits your nostro account and the balance goes up. The hub must check the **nostro balance** before releasing a payment, because if the balance is too low, the correspondent will reject it. Treasury manages nostro funding by moving money between accounts, and they need a **real time view** of every nostro balance. The hub reports each payment to the treasury system as soon as it is released, so treasury always knows the expected

entries.title: Walk through a clean SWIFT gpi payment. How does the UETR and the tracker give the customer visibility at every hop?
entries.text: SWIFT gpi works because every payment carries a **UETR**, a unique end-to-end transaction reference, and every bank in the chain updates the status against that reference. The customer sends the payment, and the sending bank creates the UETR and includes it in the **pacs.008**. As the payment moves through each intermediary, each bank updates the **gpi Tracker** with its status, so the sending bank and the customer can see exactly where the payment is. The beneficiary bank credits the account and sends a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, which appears on the tracker. The customer can check the tracker and see the payment arrived, the amount credited, and any charges deducted along the way. The sender gets a confirmation, and the **camt.053** statement matches. What makes gpi clean is the

entries.title: Walk through a clean cover method payment. How do the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover travel separately and come together at the beneficiary bank?
entries.text: The cover method works when the instruction and the money travel on separate tracks but arrive together. The sending bank creates two messages, both carrying the same **UETR**. The **pacs.008** instruction goes directly to the beneficiary bank, carrying the full customer and remittance details. The **pacs.009** with settlement method COVE goes through the correspondent chain, moving the funds between **Nostro accounts**. Each correspondent validates the cover, debits its Nostro account, and passes it on. The beneficiary bank receives the pacs.008 first, and waits for the cover to arrive. When both legs have arrived, the beneficiary bank **reconciles them** using the shared UETR, confirms the amounts match, and credits the beneficiary account. The beneficiary bank sends back a **pacs.002**

entries.title: Explain how the bank uses SWIFT gpi to track a payment when the pacs.002 has not arrived.
entries.text: **SWIFT gpi** gives the bank a tracker that is independent of the **pacs.002** flow. Every bank in the chain updates the tracker when it receives and forwards the payment, so the bank can see where the payment is even when the formal status message has not arrived. The operations team looks up the payment by its **UETR** in the gpi tracker and reads the latest status, the fees deducted at each hop, and the time the payment spent at each bank. If the tracker shows the payment was credited to the beneficiary, the bank knows the payment completed and the pacs.002 was simply lost or delayed, and the status can be updated from the tracker. If the tracker shows the payment is stuck at an intermediary, the team contacts that bank directly. If the tracker shows nothing, the payment may not have

entries.title: The gpi tracker shows the payment as credited but the internal status is still pending. Which one is right and how do you fix it?
entries.text: When the **gpi tracker** and the internal status disagree, the bank must find out which one is right. The gpi tracker is updated by every bank in the chain, so it reflects what the banks in the chain reported. The internal status reflects what the bank's own **payment hub** recorded from the **pacs.002** messages it received. A mismatch usually means a pacs.002 was lost, delayed, or not processed by the hub. The operations team checks the settlement confirmation and the **camt.053** statement first. If the statement shows the funds left the bank and the gpi tracker shows the payment was credited, then the payment did complete and the internal status is wrong. The team updates the hub status manually and investigates why the pacs.002 was missed. If the statement shows no settlement, but

entries.title: What is MT202 COV?
entries.text: An MT202 COV is the cover variant of the MT202 financial institution transfer, and it exists to solve a transparency problem. A plain MT202 moves money between banks for their own account, and it carries no customer details. If a plain MT202 were used to settle a customer payment, the intermediary banks and the creditor agent would see money moving with no idea who the underlying ordering customer or beneficiary was. That gap created a compliance and reconciliation risk, because banks could not screen the underlying parties or match the funds to the right customer instruction. The MT202 COV fixes this by carrying the cover details. It is sent through the correspondent chain to move the funds that settle an MT103 customer payment, and it includes the key customer information from the

entries.title: What is a payment investigation (MT192/195/196)?
entries.text: A payment investigation is the formal process a bank uses to find out what happened to a payment that is missing, delayed, or incorrect, and in the MT system it uses three messages. MT192 is a Request for Cancellation, sent when the sender wants a payment stopped before it settles. MT195 is a general Query, sent when the sender wants information, for example asking the beneficiary bank whether the payment was credited and on what date. MT196 is the answer to a query, sent by the bank that received the MT195, giving the status of the payment. Together, these messages form the investigation trail. In ISO 20022, the same work is done with camt.056 for a cancellation request, camt.028 for a status report, and camt.029 for the resolution of an investigation. An investigation is started when a

entries.title: A beneficiary calls to say they cannot match a payment to an invoice because the remittance information is cut off. The MT103 field 70 only shows part of the invoice number. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
entries.text: **Field 70** of the MT103, the remittance information field, holds a maximum of **four lines of 35 characters**, and anything longer is cut off. The sending bank put a long invoice reference into field 70, the message carried only the first 140 characters, and the beneficiary received a truncated reference they cannot match. The fix for this payment is to send the full reference to the beneficiary bank by a separate message, such as an **MT199** free format message, quoting the original MT103 reference so the beneficiary bank can link the two. The prevention is to use **structured remittance information** where the payment system supports it, or to keep the field 70 content short and put the full detail in the customer instruction channel, not in the SWIFT message. entries.title: A corporate customer asks why their MT103 carries a field 72, sender to receiver information, and whether they can use it to add instructions for the beneficiary bank. Explain what field 72 is for and what it must never contain.
entries.text: **Field 72** is the sender to receiver information field in the MT103. It carries instructions from the sending bank to the receiving bank, such as asking the beneficiary bank to phone the beneficiary, to hold the payment for collection, or to apply a specific value date. It is bank to bank information, and it is not part of the payment instruction to the beneficiary. The corporate customer cannot use field 72 to send a message to the beneficiary, because the beneficiary bank may not pass it on, and the beneficiary will never see it. Field 72 must never contain **payment details** that belong in other fields, such as the amount, the account number, or the remittance information, because the receiving bank systems read specific fields and may ignore field 72 entirely. It must also never

entries.title: A payment travels through three correspondent banks. The operations team is unsure whether to send an MT202 or an MT202 COV to move the funds. Explain the difference and when each one is used.
entries.text: An **MT202** is a general financial institution transfer. It moves money between banks for their own account and carries no customer details. An **MT202 COV** is the cover variant, and it carries the underlying customer information from the related **MT103**, such as the ordering customer and the beneficiary. The rule is simple: if the funds being moved settle a customer payment, use the **MT202 COV**, because every bank in the chain needs to see who the underlying customer is for **sanctions screening** and reconciliation. If the funds are the bank own money, for example a treasury transfer or a liquidity movement, use the plain **MT202**, because there is no underlying customer. In the three bank chain, the MT103 travels directly to the beneficiary bank with the full customer details,

entries.title: A treasury analyst asks for an MT910 and an MT900 to check whether two nostro payments settled yesterday. Explain what these two messages are and how the analyst uses them.
entries.text: An **MT900** is a confirmation of debit. It tells the account owner that their account has been debited, with the amount, the currency, the value date, and the reference of the original instruction. An **MT910** is a confirmation of credit, and it tells the account owner that their account has been credited, with the same details. The two messages are always sent by the **account servicing institution**, which is the bank that holds the account, to the account owner. The treasury analyst uses them to confirm that a payment actually left or arrived in the **nostro account**. If the bank sent a payment instruction and then receives an MT900, the debit is confirmed and the nostro balance can be updated. If the bank expected a receipt and receives an MT910, the credit is confirmed. If the

entries.title: A reconciliation analyst is unsure whether to use the MT940 or the MT942 for intraday nostro checking. Explain the difference between the two statements and when each one is used.
entries.text: The **MT940** is the customer statement message. It is sent at **end of day** and gives the full statement for the account: the opening balance, every debit and credit during the day, and the closing balance. It is the official record used for end of day reconciliation. The **MT942** is the interim transaction report. It is sent **during the day**, often several times, and gives the transactions since the last report, with an interim balance. The analyst uses the MT942 for **intraday monitoring**, to check that expected payments have arrived, to spot unexpected debits early, and to manage liquidity during the day. The MT940 is used for the formal end of day reconciliation, because it is complete and final. The two messages have the same structure, but the MT942 is a snapshot and the MT940

entries.title: A payment has not arrived after three days and the beneficiary bank is not responding to emails. The operations team wants to send an MT199 to chase it. Explain what an MT199 is, when it is the right message, and when a different message should be used instead.
entries.text: An **MT199** is a free format message. It is the general purpose message banks use to send information that does not fit into a structured message type. It is the right message when you need to ask a question, give information, or chase a payment, and there is no specific message type for what you want to say. For a missing payment, the MT199 should quote the original payment **reference**, the **UETR**, the amount, the currency, the value date, and the date it was sent, so the receiving bank can find it without asking for more information. But the MT199 is not always the right choice. If you want to request a **cancellation**, use the **MT192**. If you want to ask about a payment status formally, use the **MT195** enquiry. If you want to request a **recall** of funds, use the

entries.title: A customer asks their bank to cancel a payment that was sent yesterday. The bank sends an MT192 request for cancellation, but the beneficiary bank replies that the funds have already been credited to the beneficiary. What happens now?
entries.text: An **MT192** is a request for cancellation. It asks the receiving bank to stop the payment and return the funds, but it is only a request, not an instruction the receiving bank must obey. If the funds have already been **credited to the beneficiary**, the beneficiary bank cannot simply take the money back, because the beneficiary now owns it. The beneficiary bank should reply explaining the position, and the sending bank must then ask the beneficiary to agree to return the funds voluntarily. This is done through a **recall**, usually a **camt.056** message, which asks the beneficiary bank to contact the beneficiary and request the return. The beneficiary can refuse, and if they do, the sending bank has no SWIFT mechanism to force the return. The sending bank must then tell the customer

entries.title: A bank sends an MT195 to ask a correspondent bank about a missing payment. Three days later there is still no reply. Explain the MT195 and MT196 flow, what the deadlines are, and what the bank should do next.
entries.text: The **MT195** is an enquiry message. A bank sends it to ask another bank a question about a payment, such as whether it was received, whether it was credited, or why it has not arrived. The receiving bank is expected to reply with an **MT196**, which is the answer to the enquiry. The MT195 should include the original payment **reference**, the **UETR**, the amount, the currency, and the value date, so the receiving bank can identify the payment immediately. There is no universal deadline in the SWIFT rules, but market practice and **gpi service levels** expect a reply within one to two business days for a straightforward enquiry. If three days have passed with no reply, the bank should escalate: send a second MT195 marked urgent, copy the **relationship manager** at the correspondent

entries.title: A corporate treasurer wants to send 500 salary payments to their bank in a single instruction instead of 500 separate payments. Explain how the MT101 helps and what the bank does with it.
entries.text: The **MT101** is a request for transfer. It is the message a corporate customer sends to their bank to instruct multiple payments in a single message. Instead of sending 500 separate instructions, the treasurer sends one MT101 containing all 500 payment instructions, each with its own beneficiary, account, amount, and value date. The bank validates the MT101, checks that the customer account has enough funds, and then processes each instruction inside it, usually by generating individual **MT103** messages for the cross border payments or domestic clearing instructions for the local ones. The MT101 is designed for **bulk payments** such as salaries, supplier payments, and pension payments, where the same customer sends many payments on the same day. The customer must have an agreement

entries.title: An operations analyst sees an MT205 and an MT202 for the same amount on the same day and thinks it is a duplicate. Explain the difference between the two messages and why both can be legitimate.
entries.text: An **MT202** is a general financial institution transfer, used to move money between banks. An **MT205** is a financial institution transfer **execution**, and it is used when the transfer is executed by a financial institution on behalf of another financial institution. The difference is in the role of the sender. The MT202 is sent by the bank that owns the funds. The MT205 is sent by a bank that has been instructed by another bank to execute the transfer, for example when a bank uses a **correspondent** to move funds on its behalf. Both messages can appear for the same underlying movement because they describe different legs of the same chain: one bank instructs, another executes. The analyst should not treat them as duplicates. Instead, they should check the **transaction reference**,

entries.title: The MT950 end of day statement shows three entries that do not appear in the bank nostro ledger. The amounts are small but the reconciliation cannot be signed off. Walk through how you investigate the break.
entries.text: Start by confirming the **MT950** is the correct statement for the correct account and the correct value date, because a wrong account or a wrong date is the most common cause of a phantom break. Next, pull the **MT900 and MT910** confirmations for the day and check whether the three entries appear there. If they do, the entries are real and the nostro ledger is missing them. If they do not, the entries may be **charges, interest, or fees** applied by the account servicing bank, which appear on the statement but are not payment instructions and therefore never hit the payment ledger. Common examples are **correspondent charges**, **account maintenance fees**, and **interest adjustments**. Check the statement narrative for each entry: the MT950 field 86 carries the details, and a charge

entries.title: A bank agrees an FX rate with a customer for a cross border payment, but the MT300 confirmation from the counterparty shows a different rate and a different value date. What has gone wrong and how do you resolve it?
entries.text: An **MT300** is a foreign exchange confirmation. It is the message one party sends to the other to confirm the details of an FX deal: the currencies, the amounts, the **exchange rate**, the **value date**, and the settlement instructions. If the MT300 shows a different rate and a different value date from what the bank agreed with the customer, there is a **confirmation mismatch**, and the deal cannot settle as it stands. The first step is to check the original deal record: the dealer ticket, the recorded conversation, or the electronic trading platform log. That record is the evidence of what was actually agreed. Next, contact the counterparty and ask them to check their record. Most mismatches are caused by a typing error, a wrong value date convention, or a misunderstanding about which

entries.title: A customer reports a cheque as lost in the post and asks the bank to stop it. The bank sends an MT111. Explain what this message does and what the customer should expect.
entries.text: An **MT111** is a stop payment of a cheque. It is the message a bank sends to tell another bank, or to instruct its own systems, that a specific cheque must not be paid. The message carries the **cheque number**, the **amount**, the **currency**, the **account number**, and the **payee name**, so the paying bank can identify the exact cheque. Once the stop is in place, if the cheque is presented for payment, the paying bank will return it unpaid with a reason code indicating the stop. The customer should expect the stop to take effect quickly, usually the same day, but they should also know that a stop does not guarantee the cheque will never be paid: if the cheque was already presented and cleared before the stop arrived, the money has gone. The customer should also be told that a stop

entries.title: An MT103 arrives with field 50, the ordering customer field, containing only a name and no account number or address. The payment is held for compliance review. Explain why the field is incomplete, what the risks are, and how the payment gets released.
entries.text: **Field 50** in the MT103 must identify the ordering customer fully. Under the **Funds Transfer Regulation** and the **travel rule**, the ordering customer information must include the name, the account number, and the address or another identifier, so that every bank in the chain can screen the real sender. A field 50 with only a name is incomplete, and the receiving bank cannot screen the payment properly, cannot identify the sender if there is a sanctions hit, and cannot return the funds to the right account if the payment is rejected. The payment is correctly held. The fix is to ask the **sending bank** for the missing information, either by an MT199 free format message or through the **gpi Case Resolution** tool, quoting the MT103 reference and the UETR. The sending bank should reply

entries.title: During the MT to MX migration, a bank converts an MT103 into a pacs.008. The conversion drops the remittance information because the MT103 field 70 is longer than the pacs.008 allows. Explain the data problem and how the bank handles it during coexistence.
entries.text: This is a **data truncation** problem, and it is one of the most common issues in the **MT to MX migration**. The MT103 field 70 allows four lines of 35 characters, and the pacs.008 unstructured remittance information allows 140 characters, so in theory they match. But the MT103 also carries information in other fields that have no direct equivalent in the pacs.008, and the **CBPR+ usage guidelines** define exactly how each MT field maps to the MX structure. When the mapping cannot carry all the data, the bank has three options. First, use the **structured remittance information** in the pacs.008, which can carry a structured reference and additional data in a way the MT103 could not. Second, send the extra information in a separate message, such as an MT199, linked by the UETR. Third,

entries.title: What is ISO 20022?
entries.text: ISO 20022 is the global standard for exchanging electronic messages between financial institutions. It defines a common language that banks, payment systems, market infrastructures and corporates use to describe payments, securities, trade and card transactions. Instead of each system inventing its own format, ISO 20022 provides a shared dictionary of business concepts, such as debtor, creditor, amount and value date, plus a set of message definitions built on top of that dictionary. The standard is maintained by ISO Technical Committee 68 and is syntax independent in principle, but in practice almost all ISO 20022 messages today are expressed in XML. Each message type has a name, such as pacs.008 or pain.001, and a published schema that spells out exactly which elements are mandatory,

entries.title: What is CBPR+?
entries.text: CBPR+ stands for Cross Border Payments and Reporting Plus. It is the working group that defines how ISO 20022 is used for cross border payments on the SWIFT network. ISO 20022 itself is a broad standard with many optional elements, and different banks could implement it in different ways. CBPR+ exists to prevent that fragmentation: it publishes usage guidelines that say exactly which elements are mandatory, which are optional, and which rules apply for cross border payments, so that a pacs.008 sent by a bank in Singapore is understood the same way by a bank in Germany. The group is made up of banks, market infrastructures and SWIFT, and its guidelines are the practical rulebook for the migration. They cover message versions, character sets, address formats, charge bearer rules, and how

entries.title: A payment engine produces ISO 20022 pacs.008 messages but the downstream clearing system still expects MT103. How do you handle the transformation, and what is the biggest risk?
entries.text: Start from the message the engine produces and the message the clearing house expects. The engine works in **ISO 20022** and produces a **pacs.008**. The clearing house may still expect **MT103** on the SWIFT network, or it may accept pacs.008 natively. The transformation happens in a **mapping layer** between the engine and the clearing interface. Every field in pacs.008 must map to a field in MT103, and the mapping is not one to one. For example, pacs.008 carries structured debtor and creditor addresses with separate fields for street, town and country. MT103 field 59 has a limited character set and no structure, so the mapper must flatten the address and truncate it without losing the town and country. The **charge bearer** in pacs.008 maps to field 71A in MT103, OUR, SHA or BEN. The

entries.title: How do you explain ISO 20022 migration to a business stakeholder?
entries.text: I explain ISO 20022 migration as a change of language, not a change of banking. Today the bank speaks one language for payments, the old MT messages, and it needs to learn a new language, the MX messages. The new language is richer: it carries more information, structured addresses, longer references and clearer data. The migration means the bank must be able to send and receive the new messages, translate between the old and the new during the transition, and handle the cases where the other bank has not migrated yet. I explain the business impact in plain terms: the new messages let the bank carry more information about a payment, which improves reconciliation and reduces exceptions. I explain the timeline: the migration happens in phases, and there are deadlines set by SWIFT and the

entries.title: What is SEPA?
entries.text: SEPA, the Single Euro Payments Area, is the framework that makes euro payments work the same way across Europe. Before SEPA, a payment from Germany to France was a cross border payment with different formats, timelines and charges from a domestic payment. SEPA harmonised that: within the SEPA area, which covers the eurozone plus several other European countries, a euro payment is treated the same whether it stays inside one country or crosses a border. The framework is governed by the European Payments Council and supported by EU regulation. SEPA defines three main payment instruments. SEPA Credit Transfer, SCT, is the standard euro credit transfer, where the payer instructs their bank to send money to the beneficiary. SEPA Direct Debit, SDD, lets a creditor collect money from a debtor

entries.title: What is SEPA Instant?
entries.text: SEPA Instant, formally SEPA Instant Credit Transfer or SCT Inst, is the real time version of the SEPA Credit Transfer. It is a scheme from the European Payments Council that lets euro payments settle within seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, between accounts in the SEPA area. The target is a maximum of ten seconds from the payer bank sending the payment to the beneficiary bank confirming receipt, and most payments complete much faster. The scheme went live in 2017 and has grown steadily as more banks and payment service providers joined. The mechanics are straightforward in concept and demanding in practice. The payer bank sends an SCT Inst instruction, the beneficiary bank must respond within the time limit, confirming that the account exists and the funds are credited or

entries.title: Your bank is a direct participant in SEPA. A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. Walk through what happens from instruction to settlement in under 10 seconds.
entries.text: The customer submits the payment through the channel, and the **payment hub** validates it, checks sanctions, and confirms the beneficiary bank is reachable for **SEPA Instant**. The hub formats the payment as a **pacs.008** and sends it to the beneficiary bank through the **SEPA Instant** clearing system, usually **TIPS** or a private clearing house. The whole journey must complete within 10 seconds, and the clearing system enforces a 20-second maximum. The beneficiary bank receives the pacs.008, validates the account, and must respond within the time limit. If it accepts, it credits the customer immediately and sends back a **pacs.002** with **ACSC** status. Settlement between the banks happens in central bank money through TIPS at the same time, so there is no deferred settlement. If

entries.title: Walk through a clean SEPA credit transfer, from the customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. What makes the SEPA scheme work so smoothly?
entries.text: A SEPA credit transfer is clean because the scheme is standardised. The customer submits the instruction through their bank, and the bank validates it, checking the **IBAN** format, the balance, and the sanctions lists. The bank sends a **pacs.008** to the beneficiary bank, either directly or through a clearing system. The pacs.008 carries the IBAN, the amount, the end-to-end reference, and the remittance information. The beneficiary bank receives it, validates the IBAN, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. For a standard SEPA credit transfer, the funds arrive by the next business day. For a **SEPA Instant** payment, the funds arrive within ten seconds, and the beneficiary bank must confirm receipt with a pacs.002 carrying ACSC status within that

entries.title: A customer sends a SEPA credit transfer and it comes back rejected with reason code AC01. The customer insists the IBAN is correct. Explain what AC01 means and how you help the customer fix it.
entries.text: **AC01** means incorrect account number. The receiving bank checked the **IBAN** in the payment and found that it does not match a valid account. The customer may have typed the IBAN correctly as they see it, but the problem is usually a small error: a digit transposed, a character missing, or the IBAN copied from an old document after the account changed. The first step is to ask the customer to check the IBAN against the source, such as the beneficiary invoice or the beneficiary bank statement, character by character. The IBAN has a built in **check digit**, so a typing error can be detected, but it cannot tell you what the correct IBAN is. If the IBAN is genuinely correct and the payment still rejects with AC01, the account may be **closed**, or the beneficiary bank may not accept SEPA

entries.title: A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. The money leaves their account, but the beneficiary bank does not confirm within 10 seconds and the payment times out. Explain what happens to the money and what the bank must do.
entries.text: A **SEPA Instant** payment must complete within **10 seconds**. If the beneficiary bank does not confirm receipt in that time, the payment **times out**. The money has already left the payer account, so the bank must now find out what happened to it. The payer bank sends an **investigation** message to the beneficiary bank, asking whether the payment was credited, rejected, or never received. There are three outcomes. If the beneficiary bank credited the payment but the confirmation was delayed, the payment is complete and the payer bank tells the customer it arrived. If the beneficiary bank rejected the payment, the funds must be **returned** to the payer, usually within one business day. If the beneficiary bank never received the payment, the payer bank must trace it through the

entries.title: A customer sees a direct debit on their account that they do not recognise. They say they never signed a mandate. Explain how a SEPA Direct Debit works, what the customer rights are, and how the bank handles the dispute.
entries.text: A **SEPA Direct Debit**, or SDD, lets a creditor, such as a utility company, collect money from the debtor account, but only if the debtor has signed a **mandate** giving permission. The mandate states the creditor name, the amount or the collection pattern, and the debtor account. Without a valid mandate, the collection is not authorised. If the customer says they never signed a mandate, the bank must ask the creditor bank for a copy of the **mandate** and check it against the customer details. The customer has strong rights: under the SEPA rules, they can request a **refund** of an unauthorised direct debit within **13 months**, and the bank must return the money within **10 business days** of the claim while it investigates. If the mandate is valid and the customer simply forgot, the

entries.title: A SEPA Instant payment is credited to the beneficiary, but the payer then discovers the payment was sent to the wrong account because of a typing error. The payer asks for the money back. Explain the recall process and why the beneficiary can refuse.
entries.text: A **SEPA Instant** payment is **irrevocable** once it is credited. The payer cannot cancel it through the payment system, because the money has already moved and the beneficiary bank has confirmed receipt. The only route is a **recall**, which is a request from the payer bank to the beneficiary bank, asking the beneficiary to return the funds voluntarily. The beneficiary bank contacts the beneficiary and explains the situation, but the beneficiary is **not obliged** to return the money. If the beneficiary agrees, the funds are sent back, usually as a new payment, and the case is closed. If the beneficiary refuses, or does not respond, the payer bank has no power to force the return through the SEPA scheme. The payer options are then to contact the beneficiary directly, or to take **legal

entries.title: A customer is about to send a SEPA payment and sees a warning that the payee name does not match the account number. The name is almost right, just one letter different. Explain what verification of payee does and what the customer should do.
entries.text: **Verification of payee** is a check that runs before a SEPA payment is sent. The bank compares the **payee name** the payer typed against the name registered to the **IBAN**, and it returns one of three results: a **match**, a **close match**, or **no match**. A close match means the name is almost right, often because of a spelling difference, a missing middle name, or a company trading name instead of its legal name. The customer should stop and check: is this the right person, is the IBAN copied correctly, and does the close match make sense? If the customer is sure the details are right, they can proceed, but they should know the bank has warned them. If the customer is not sure, they should contact the payee and confirm the name and IBAN before sending. A **no match** is a stronger

entries.title: A customer submits a SEPA credit transfer on Friday evening and expects the money to arrive the same day. Explain how SEPA value dates and cut-off times work, and when the beneficiary will actually be paid.
entries.text: A standard **SEPA Credit Transfer**, or SCT, is not instant. It is processed on **business days**, and the value date, the day the beneficiary is credited, depends on when the payment is submitted and on the **cut-off time** of the payer bank. If the customer submits the payment on Friday evening after the cut-off, the bank will process it on the next business day, which is Monday, and the beneficiary will be credited on Monday, or Tuesday if the beneficiary bank takes a day to process it. The SEPA rule is that the payment must reach the beneficiary bank by the end of the next business day after it is accepted, so a Friday evening payment is not late, it is simply queued for Monday. If the customer needs the money to arrive on Friday, they should use **SEPA Instant**, which settles in

entries.title: A corporate customer needs to pay a supplier 150,000 euro immediately, but their bank SEPA Instant limit is 100,000 euro. Explain the options and the risks of splitting the payment.
entries.text: The **SEPA Instant** scheme has a maximum amount per transaction, and many banks set their own lower limit, often **100,000 euro**, for risk and liquidity reasons. The customer has three options. First, ask the bank to raise the **limit** temporarily for this payment, which the bank may do after checking the customer and the beneficiary. Second, split the payment into two **SEPA Instant** payments, for example 100,000 euro and 50,000 euro. This works, but it creates a **reconciliation** problem, because the supplier receives two payments instead of one and must match both to the same invoice. Third, send the payment as a standard **SEPA Credit Transfer**, which has no scheme limit, but which will not arrive instantly and may take until the next business day. Splitting the payment also

entries.title: A biller collects a SEPA Direct Debit and the customer bank returns it. The biller wants to know why. Explain the SDD R-transactions: return, refund, reversal, and reject, and what each one means for the biller.
entries.text: **R-transactions** are the exception messages in **SEPA Direct Debit**. Each one means something different, and the biller must handle them differently. A **reject** happens before the collection is processed, usually because the debtor account is closed, the IBAN is wrong, or the mandate is invalid. The biller receives the reject quickly and can fix the data. A **return** happens after the collection, because there were insufficient funds, or the debtor bank refused the debit. The biller can try to collect again, but should check with the debtor first. A **refund** is requested by the debtor: for an authorised collection, the debtor has **8 weeks** to ask for a refund, no questions asked, and the bank must return the money. A **reversal** is requested by the creditor bank, usually

entries.title: A bank in Sweden, which is in SEPA but does not use the euro, wants to offer SEPA Instant payments to its customers. Explain the challenges and what the bank must build.
entries.text: Sweden is in **SEPA** but does not use the euro, which creates a specific challenge: the customer account is in **Swedish krona**, but the SEPA Instant payment must settle in **euro**. The bank must therefore offer a **currency conversion** as part of the payment, converting krona to euro at the point of sending, and it must show the customer the exchange rate and the converted amount before they confirm. The bank must also be **reachable** for SEPA Instant, which means connecting to a clearing system such as **TIPS** or the EBA Clearing RT1 system, and being available 24 hours a day, because instant payments never sleep. The bank must handle the **liquidity** in euro, holding enough euro in its settlement account to cover outgoing instant payments at any time, including weekends when the

entries.title: A fraudster tricks a customer into sending a SEPA Instant payment to a mule account. The money is moved on within minutes. Explain why instant payments are attractive to fraudsters and what banks do to stop it.
entries.text: **SEPA Instant** payments are attractive to fraudsters because they are **irrevocable** and they settle in **seconds**. Once the money is credited to the mule account, the fraudster can move it on to another account, withdraw it, or convert it, all before the victim realises they have been tricked. There is no time to stop the payment, because there is no clearing window to intervene in. Banks fight this in three ways. First, **verification of payee** checks the payee name against the IBAN before the payment is sent, and warns the customer if there is a mismatch. Second, **transaction monitoring** looks for mule account patterns: an account that receives money and immediately sends it on, an account with no normal activity that suddenly receives a large payment, or an account linked to

entries.title: Your bank is choosing how to settle SEPA Instant payments: through TIPS or through EBA Clearing RT1. Explain the difference between the two and how the bank decides.
entries.text: **TIPS**, the TARGET Instant Payment Settlement service, is run by the **Eurosystem** and settles SEPA Instant payments in **central bank money**, in real time, 24 hours a day. Each payment is settled individually and immediately, with finality at the moment of settlement. **RT1**, run by **EBA Clearing**, is a clearing system that also settles in real time, but it uses a **prefunded** model: participating banks hold funds in a technical account, and payments are settled against those prefunded balances. The difference matters for **liquidity** and for **risk**. With TIPS, the bank needs liquidity in its central bank account, and settlement is in central bank money, which is the safest form of settlement. With RT1, the bank needs to prefund the technical account, and the prefunding must

entries.title: Your bank still runs a legacy domestic payment format alongside SEPA. The board wants to retire the legacy format and move everything to ISO 20022. Explain the migration and the risks of running two formats in parallel.
entries.text: Migrating from a **legacy domestic format** to **ISO 20022** means changing the message format for every payment the bank sends and receives. The legacy format is usually a fixed length file or a proprietary message, while ISO 20022 uses **XML** with structured data, including structured addresses, purpose codes, and rich remittance information. The migration has three parts. First, the bank must **map** every field in the legacy format to the ISO 20022 equivalent, and decide what to do with fields that have no equivalent. Second, the bank must update its **customer channels**, because the data the customer provides must now be structured, and the bank must validate it before sending. Third, the bank must **test** with every counterparty, because a payment that is valid in the legacy

entries.title: What is settlement risk?
entries.text: Settlement risk is the risk that one party to a payment or transaction does not deliver what it owes when it is due, even though the other party has already delivered its side. In payments, it is the risk that a bank credits its customer or releases goods or securities before it has actually received the funds from the sending bank, and then the sending bank fails to pay. A simple example shows the problem. Bank A sends a payment instruction to Bank B, and Bank B credits its customer immediately in the expectation that Bank A will settle later that day. If Bank A becomes insolvent before settlement, Bank B has paid out money it will never receive. Bank B bears the loss, and its customer keeps the funds. Settlement risk is largest in systems where there is a long gap between the payment

entries.title: What is CHIPS netting?
entries.text: CHIPS netting is the process by which the Clearing House Interbank Payments System offsets payments between banks so that only the net amount needs to be settled at the end of the day. During the operating day, banks send payment instructions to CHIPS, which records them in a central queue. CHIPS does not settle each payment immediately. Instead, it keeps a running total of what each bank owes to every other bank. If Bank A owes Bank B 100 million dollars and Bank B owes Bank A 80 million dollars, the net position is 20 million dollars from A to B. CHIPS also uses a liquidity saving mechanism. It holds payments in a queue and releases them when an offsetting payment arrives, so that the net amount is smaller and less liquidity is needed. Each participant prefunds an account at the Federal

entries.title: How does a bank manage cut-off times across multiple clearing systems?
entries.text: A large bank connects to many clearing systems: Faster Payments, CHAPS, BACS, SEPA, Fedwire, CHIPS and SWIFT. Each one has its own cut off time, the last moment a payment can be sent and still settle that day. The bank manages this with a cut off calendar. For each clearing system, the bank records the cut off time, the time zone and the value date rule. The payment hub reads this calendar when it routes a payment. If a payment arrives before the cut off, it is sent the same day. If it arrives after the cut off, the hub either holds it for the next day or rejects it, depending on the product rules. The customer is told the value date so they know when the beneficiary will receive the money. The complexity comes when a payment crosses time zones. A payment sent from London at 4pm for a US

entries.title: How does your bank actually connect to a clearing house? Explain the technical path from the payment hub to the clearing system.
entries.text: The bank does not send payments directly from the branch or the app to the clearing house. The **channel** captures the instruction and passes it to the **payment hub**. The hub is the single control point. It validates the instruction, checks sanctions and fraud, applies the charge option, and decides the clearing route. Then it formats the payment into the clearing system's message standard, for example **ISO 20022 pacs.008** for most modern clearing systems, or the local format the clearing house requires. From the hub, the payment travels over a secure connection to the clearing house. For **SWIFT**, that connection is the SWIFT network, and the bank's **BIC** identifies it. For domestic clearing such as **CHAPS** or **Faster Payments**, the bank connects through the Bank of England

entries.title: The clearing house is down during a settlement window. What does the bank do with payments queued for that window?
entries.text: The first step is to confirm the outage is real and not a problem on the bank's own side. The operations team checks the clearing house status page and contacts the clearing house service desk. Once confirmed, the **payment hub** holds all payments due for that window in the queue. Nothing is released, because there is nowhere to send it. The bank must not try an alternative route without checking, because the payment may already have been accepted by the clearing house before it went down. The bank then communicates. Clients with time-critical payments are told the clearing house is down and given a revised estimate. Treasury is told, because the funding plan for the day changes. When the clearing house comes back, the bank releases the queued payments in priority order, usually

entries.title: Your bank has a large FX payment settling through CLS. How does CLS remove settlement risk, and what happens if one leg fails?
entries.text: **CLS**, Continuous Linked Settlement, removes **Herstatt risk**, which is the risk that one side of an FX trade settles and the other side does not. The bank submits both legs of the FX payment to CLS. CLS holds both legs and settles them simultaneously, payment versus payment. If one leg cannot settle, neither leg settles. That is the core protection. The bank funds its CLS account in each currency before the settlement window, and CLS nets the flows so the bank only funds the net amount, not the gross. If one leg fails, CLS does not settle the trade. The bank is told which currency is short and by how much. The bank then has to fund the short leg, usually by borrowing in the market or moving funds from another account. If it cannot fund in time, the trade is deferred to the next

entries.title: A payment is stuck in the RTGS queue because the bank does not have enough balance. How does queue resolution work, and what can the bank do to release it?
entries.text: When a bank sends a payment through **RTGS** and its **central bank settlement account** does not have enough balance, the payment does not fail. It sits in the **RTGS queue**. The central bank's queue resolution mechanism looks at all queued payments across all banks and tries to find a set that can settle together, because one bank's outgoing payment is another bank's incoming payment. If a group of queued payments can be settled by offsetting them against each other, the central bank releases them as a batch. This is called **gridlock resolution** or multilateral offset. The bank can also act on its own. It can add funds to the settlement account, either by moving money from another account or by borrowing from the central bank's **intraday liquidity facility** against collateral. It

entries.title: The bank receives a settlement confirmation from the clearing house. What does the bank do with it, and how does it update the payment status?
entries.text: The settlement confirmation arrives as a status message, usually a **pacs.002** with **ACSC** status, meaning the payment has been accepted and settled. The **payment hub** receives it and matches it to the original payment using the message reference and the **UETR**. The hub checks that the amount, currency, and value date match the original instruction. If they match, the hub updates the payment status to settled and posts the accounting entries, debiting the customer account and crediting the settlement account. The hub then pushes the status update to the **channel**, so the customer can see the payment as completed. If the payment was a corporate payment, the hub may also send a confirmation through the corporate banking portal or an **MT900** confirmation message. If the

entries.title: A payment is sent with the wrong settlement method in the pacs.008. What goes wrong downstream, and how do you fix it?
entries.text: The **settlement method** in the **pacs.008** tells the clearing system how the payment should settle, for example through the central bank, through a correspondent, or through a clearing house. If it is wrong, the payment can go to the wrong settlement account or be rejected by the clearing system. The first sign is usually a **pacs.002** with an **RJCT** status, or the payment sitting in the hub with no settlement confirmation. The operations team checks the pacs.008 against the static data for that corridor. Each corridor, meaning each currency and destination combination, has a defined settlement method, and the hub should have picked it automatically. If the static data is wrong, the fix is to correct the static data so every future payment on that corridor uses the right method. If

entries.title: A clearing house rejects a batch of payments for a formatting error. How does the bank find the error, fix it, and resubmit?
entries.text: When a clearing house rejects a batch, the first step is to read the rejection message carefully. It usually names the error, such as a schema failure, an invalid field, or a limit breach. The operations team pulls the rejected file and identifies which payments failed and which, if any, were accepted. The accepted ones are left alone, because resubmitting them would create duplicates. The team then finds the root cause. If it is a **formatting error**, the fix is in the hub's message mapping for that clearing system. If it is a data error, such as an invalid **BIC** or a missing mandatory field, the fix is in the source data or the validation rules. The failed payments are corrected, revalidated, and resubmitted as new instructions with new message IDs, keeping the same **UETR** for

entries.title: A customer payment is due to settle on a day the clearing house is closed for a holiday. What happens to the value date and the customer?
entries.text: When the clearing house is closed for a holiday, no settlement happens that day. The **payment hub** checks the clearing calendar before accepting the payment and warns the client that the value date will move. If the payment was already submitted, the hub holds it in the queue and releases it on the next working day. The value date becomes the next working day, and the customer is told the new date. The bank must be careful with the customer promise. If the client was told the payment would settle on the holiday, that promise is now broken, and the bank should have caught it at submission. The channel should show the correct value date before the client confirms, not after. For standing instructions and scheduled payments, the bank's system should automatically move the value date to the

entries.title: Explain settlement finality. At what point can the bank be certain the money has moved and cannot be reversed by the clearing house?
entries.text: **Settlement finality** means the payment has settled and cannot be reversed by the clearing system. For **RTGS** payments, finality happens the moment the payment settles across the **central bank settlement account**. The sending bank's account is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited, and that movement is final. The receiving bank can then credit its customer knowing the funds are genuinely there. For other systems, finality happens at different points. In **Faster Payments**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer immediately, but the interbank settlement is deferred, so the bank is taking a small risk until the net settlement cycle completes. In **CHIPS**, finality happens when the payment is released from the queue and settled through the prefunded account. In

entries.title: The clearing system is down during the settlement window. Payments are queuing in the payment hub and the cut-off is approaching. How do you handle a clearing system outage?
entries.text: A clearing outage means payments cannot settle, but they can still be accepted, validated, and queued. The first job is to protect the queue and keep customers informed. I confirm the outage through the clearing system status page and the **pacs.002** responses, because a missing response can look like an outage when it is actually a timeout. I check which payments are affected, separating those already settled from those still queued. For queued payments, I verify that the payment hub is holding them safely with their original value dates and instructions intact. I switch on **manual monitoring** of the queue, because automatic retry during an outage can create duplicates when the system comes back.
